maintopic: STATEMENT REGARDING IRREGULARITIES IN PEACE RIVER ELECTION

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: STATEMENT REGARDING IRREGULARITIES IN PEACE RIVER ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege.
2126	COMMONS
Privilege-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
On April 2 there appeared in various newspapers reports of the trial of Baldy Robb at Edmonton, Alberta. He was charged with and convicted of irregularities in the performance of his duties as deputy returning officer at No. 4 poll, near Brule, in the Peace River constituency at the federal election on October 29 last. Mr. Justice Walsh presided at the trial and is reported in the Edmonton Journal of April 1 as having said when addressing the jury:
The fraud which was alleged to have been perpetrated was or.e of a very serious character. In all the history of the Dominion there has never been an instance of such a glaring attempt to deprive citizens of their rights as voters. If this was true, then ninety voters had been deprived of their franchise. Mr. Collins had been deprived of his seat m the Dominion parliament, and the people of this riding had been deprived of their rights in having a man of their choice to represent them at Ottawa. . . . There was the evidence of the 111 people who had sworn that they voted for Collins on that day. This was the foundation on which the crown had built their structure. There was a possibility that these people might have committed wholesale perjury. Personally, said His Lordship, he found it hard to believe that a number of apparently respectable people like these had perjured themselves through fear of their employers.
In order to appeal to my sense of fairness the Ottawa Journal on April 3 in an editorial headed "Should Mr. Kennedy vote" strips this statement of Justice Walsh of all qualification, and makes this statement:
The fraud which was perpetrated was one of a very serious character. In all the history of the Dominion there had never been an instance of such a glaring attempt to deprive citizens of their rights as voters. Ninety citizens had been deprived of their franchise.
The words "If this was true," and the reference to the possibility of wholesale perjury are omitted, and then the editorial is built up to convince me that I have no moral right to sit in parliament or to vote for or against government measures. I intend to do both.
The statement of Mr. Justice Walsh, even if it were as the Ottawa Journal has it, was made at a trial held in connection with one poll out of 278. I claim now and have claimed ever since the early part of November that other irregularities in Peace River cost me more votes than the alleged switching of ballots at Brule cost Collins, even assuming that none of my ballots were switched at that point. The final results of No. 4 poll were: Collins (Conservative) 22; Kennedy, 12; Rae (Liberal) 127. It would therefore appear from the evidence that 89 votes were switched to Rae. I was elected by a plurality of 17 votes over Collins and 41 votes over Rae.
Six neighbouring polls in one district had all the election machinery set up and ballot boxes mailed addressed to the deputy returning officer, but no deputy returning officers

had been appointed. Three of these polls through the initiative of the people themselves were opened and the total results were: Collins, 15; Kennedy, 114; Rae, 15. The other three boxes remained in the nearest post office all day but no poll was held. At the latter three polls 225 persons had the right to vote. Many of them went to look for the polling place and of course found none. My information is that the vote there would have been divided similarly to the vote at the three polls that <vere opened.
The recount in Peace River was completed im December 19. A representative of the Conservative candidate asked me if, in view of the Brule situation, I would not consent to go through the first session of parliament and then resign. I told him at once that in my judgment owing to other election irregularities I had lost at least as many votes as Collins and that the proper course to follow, if they were not satisfied, was to petition under the Controverted Elections Act.

maintopic: STATEMENT REGARDING IRREGULARITIES IN PEACE RIVER ELECTION
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman tell us the name of that gentleman?

maintopic: STATEMENT REGARDING IRREGULARITIES IN PEACE RIVER ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Milner who was
acting for Mr. Collins. Instead of this they appealed to a Supreme court judge to have the poll at Paddle River, where the vote stood Collins, 11; Kennedy, 87; Rae, 5, thrown out, and 103 voters disfranchised on the technical ground that the deputy returning officer was not properly sworn in. It appears that the commissioner was not present when the deputy signed the oath form. In any event with sixty days in which to act under the Controverted Elections Act nothing was done by the Conservatives.
However a petition against my return has been filed in the Supreme Court of Alberta under the Controverted Elections Act by J. B. Page of Coalspur, through the legal firm of the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Cross).
If the Conservatives have now any desire to act and Page fails to press his petition I am informed that they can do so.
The petition charges me with everything the election act prohibits and asks that I be completely disfranchised. In view of this fact, even if I were otherwise disposed to resign I would not do so until the matter was disposed of. If no one else does so, I fully intend to press for action in this matter as soon as this session is over.
But, Mr. Speaker, I cannot resign. Chapter 11, section 8, of the Revised Statutes of Canada 1906, reads as follows:
No member shall tender his resignation while his election is lawfully contested, or until after the ex-

Privilege-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
piration of the time during which it may by law be contested on other grounds than corruption or bribery.
Until this petition is disposed of I intend to assume all the responsibilities and exercise all the privileges of a member of the House of Commons. I do not wish, however, to take shelter behind the petition or the law. I would refuse to resign even if there were no petition. I would not resign if I could and could not if I would. And let me say to that section of the press that has alternately flattered and threatened me during these last few days:	I do not value their praise nor
fear their threats. I defy them.
There is a bigger question involved than the Peace River seat or the government in power. Northern Alberta has come through an election that has shown the existence of elements that must be rooted out of our political contests if respect for our parliamentary institutions is to remain. The chief question is how to do this. If I can help, neither the loss of the Peace River seat nor even disfranchisement would worry me in the least degree. And let me say that if this end can be served by unseating me, I will hold no grudge against anyone taking action to do so.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: STATEMENT REGARDING IRREGULARITIES IN PEACE RIVER ELECTION
speechtext:
This is a matter that
affects not only the privilege of the hon. member (Mr. Kennedy, Peace River) himself, but the privileges of the House as such. I do not propose to comment at any length on the subject now. The House was not apprised until this very moment of the stand which the hon. gentleman purposed taking; prior to meeting we had only a rumour upon which of course we could not decide, much less act. I should not let the occasion pass, however, without saying that I cannot agree with the reasoning advanced by the hon. member for Peace River, and I must take issue most flatly with the conclusion to which he comes.
It is true that under the House of Commons Act, while a petition stands against him in the courts the right of resignation is not the hon. member's. But the act of resignation is one thing and the act of exercising his functions here as a member and a voter is another. The hon. member now stands in this position, that the official and judicial findings as respects the election in his county show that he was not returned a member of this House.

maintopic: STATEMENT REGARDING IRREGULARITIES IN PEACE RIVER ELECTION
speechtext: That was not the trial of an election petition.

maintopic: STATEMENT REGARDING IRREGULARITIES IN PEACE RIVER ELECTION
speechtext:
There is no charge
against the hon. member himself of malpractice, nor is there any charge that there was any dishonesty on the part of anyone else on his behalf. The only fault to be found with the hon. member exercising his functions is that he was not elected. The hon. member argues that but for "other irregularities" he would have been elected, and I must pause to comment on the use of the word "irregularities" which he was benevolent enough to apply to one who has now been convicted of a gross criminal offence against the code of Canada and is in consequence under a sentence to the penitentiary. The hon. member's euphemism may have some significance, but it does not at all detract from the heinousness of the offence. He argues that but for "other irregularities", namely, the fact that certain polls were not voted at all that the government's agents failed to send boxes to those polls, he would have been elected inasmuch as he is able he believes, to read the minds of the voters well enough to know that they would have voted for him. How weak and feeble this is by way of defence is evident on its mere statement. The fact is that from the votes polled the official judicial findings are that the hon. member was not returned, but that Mr. Collins secured the largest number of votes and has therefore the right to sit in this House. Under these circumstances it is difficult indeed to understand how the hon, member can feel himself playing his right part, in relation not only to his constituents but to this House, in continuing to exercise the functions of a member; and still more difficult it is to understand his reasoning by which he throws the blame for the circumstance that he did not obtain enough votes upon irregularities by officers of this government when the fact is. as he must admit, that he owes his alleged return to frauds and crimes perpetrated by a deputy returning officer acting on behalf of the same government. The hon. member represents those frauds in this House to-day, and he represents the men who perpetrated them:	He is here because of them, and I
think he would have done himself more credit had he realized the position, and, pending at least the event of the action under the Controverted Elections Act, retire from membership in the meantime. The subject is one which undoubtedly will require further consideration and certainly this House has the right to pass upon it. It has that right, and at the first convenient opportunity it will be called upon to exercise it.
Privilege-Mr. McPhee

PRIVILEGE-Mr. McPHEE

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved the second reading of Bill No. 16, to authorize advances to settlers in crown lands.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, we had a pretty
thorough discussion uipon the resolution itself, and the main objections taken were to the amount to be loaned each year and the absence of a time limit. I have amended section 9 to meet the criticisms offered by-reducing the total amount of loans per annum to $1,000,000. and by restricting the operation of the act to five years. .

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to have the bill go into committee, but I am not prepared to let the statement made by the minister go unchallenged. Our objections are much wider than he stated. Especially I 'wish to raise the question here that the moneys to be applied upon these loans should be voted by parliament, and should not be statutorily taken out of the treasury without being included in the estimates.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of the
House to adopt the motion?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are some abjections to this 14011-136
bill which I did not express when the resolution was under discussion, thinking perhaps that when the bill was brought down in its amended form those objections would disappear; but they have not. I should like to draw the attention of the House to the definition of crown lands:
Any land suitable and available for settlement, lying within fifteen miles of a railway-
That will 'prevent the operation of the act in a large portion of British Columbia where the crown lands for the most part are in those portions of the province where there is no railway at all. Seven-eighths of the district that I represent are without any railways, but are served by water and a large portion contains land very suitable for agriculture. The same remarks apply to the district of Skeena, except in the northern portion, where the old Canadian Northern line is operating. The same is true to a large extent of the district of North Vancouver, except in the extreme south. I would suggest the introduction of the words:
-or steamer landing
After the words, " within fifteen miles of a railway." I have in mind a particular valley very suitable for settlement which has a steamer service four times a week. It is provincial crown land to a large extent, and the settlers in co-operation with the provincial authorities might take advantage of the act in that district, but if they have to wait until a railway comes there it may not be possible for them to do anythin^ for twenty years. Then there are a number of large and fairly important irfands devoted to or suitable for agriculture-for instance, those lying in the gulf of Georgia running as far north as Prince Rupert. The Queen Charlotte islands have large possibilities agriculturally. It will be a very long time before any railways are built on those islands. They contain a lot of fine land suitable for settlement under this act, but of course their sole transportation from the islands is by water.
Then I see in section 3 it is proposed to:
Make a loan to any settler on the security of improvements made by such settler-
If the exact wording is to be adhered to the act will	be	nugatory, because if	a manhas made a	thousand dollars worth	of	improvements he is fairly- well started and does not need any loan. If, on the other hand, as we are told by word of mouth, it is the intention of	the	government to lend	on	thesame system	as	the progress loans under	the
Soldier Settlement Act, it would be all right, because the Soldier Settlement Board, by their



Advances to Settlers
officials, first outlined the manner in which the money was to be spent. Then if the loan was for say $1,000, they would make progress payments-that is, after the settler had done $200 worth, they would pay him that sum, and so on. In that way he could live while carrying out his improvements. But this intention is not so expressed, and as the section stands it would imply that the man would have to have made a thousand dollars worth of improvements made before he would be entitled to a loan. The first thousand dollars worth of improvements is much harder to finance than the second thousand, because for the further improvements he has greater security to offer. Sub-section (a) provides that the money will be loaned:
To a settler who is a Canadian citizen.
This is the first time that we have had presented a scheme to promote land settlement which applies to those now in Canada; generally it is confined to foreigners coming in. Perhaps such a man, brought up on a farm but now living in a town, would like to get back on the land, having become tired of urban life. I believe if carried out properly this scheme will result in attracting a considerable number of people from the cities back to the land.
Section 4 deals with settlement loan committees. I cannot see much to commend in the establishment and management of these committees. It says:
A settlement loan committee shall consist of not less than two and not more than three persons-
Suppose the two do not agree with respect to an application for a loan, what is to happen? There is no provision made for this contingency. Then it says that these three persons must be in the employ of the Dominion government or of any provincial government, which apparently means that they must- he already in government service in some other capacity, because in a lower section it says they shall not receive any salary or remuneration in addition to that otherwise received. Very well; we will deal with the provincial officials first. Except in the northern part there are in British Columbia no Dominion crown lands at all, and this will be largely a matter of provincial crown lands. The proposition apparently is to employ the services of three provincial officials who are paid for doing something else and whose time is no doubt fully occupied with those duties. This Dominion government-with the consent, no doubt, of the province-is to give those men instructions and orders as to what they are to do. According to the bill one man must be either the Dominion lands agent

or the provincial crown lands agent; in British Columbia the term used is "government agent" and that gentleman has many duties to perform. When he is fulfilling those duties is he to be directed, by some power utterly foreign to that which employs him, to go perhaps a hundred miles away and do something else? He will not feel like hurrying to obey the orders of someone who has no authority over him and is not paving him. I think the wording is unfortunate and that a better scheme could be devised.
Then I see by subsection 7 of section 5 that all settlement loans shall be extended under the direction or control of the minister. Of what minister? I presume it is the minister under this act, the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Stewart, .Edmonton), That, in conjunction with what I have already said about the formation of the committees, leads me to this point: I urge the government to deal with this matter through either one department or the other, and not jumble it up between two departments The Department of Immigration and 'Colonization has had practically no experience in the handling of Dominion lands or loans to farmers, while the Soldier Settlement Board has had a very-extensive and somewhat dearly bought experience. They made many mistakes and profited by them, and are much more qualified to carry out the loans under this bill; they have men trained to deal with these very things. Now we are apparently going to take it away from these men-although we are told verbally that their opinions will be asked. That will mean a system of dual control, with the two departments passing the buck from one to the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: I think my hon. friend is under a misapprehension, if he will permit me to interrupt. The Soldier Settlement Board is now under the Department of Immigration and Colonization, and the minister mentioned in the bill is merely the minister in charge of that board. maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
The ministerial head may be the same but nevertheless there are two distinct departments. If it is to be done by the Soldier Settlement Board why not say so and put the whole power in their hands?
Mr. 'STEWART (Edmonton): The Soldier Settlement Board will not be curtailed in their functions or powers; they are now under the Minister of Immigration, and the minister is merely mentioned as the head of the department.

Advances to Settlers

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Then why creat these elusive committees? Why not leave it as before, under the Soldier Settlement Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: There is no objection in the world; that was not thought of when the act was drafted.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: It is an afterthought, then, to put it into the hands of the Soldier Settlement Board?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
No, that
was the intention all the time. My hon. friend will notice in all these acts that the minister in charge of the department is the minister mentioned. The machinery functions under the board. If my hon. friend objects to the wording there will be no objection to inserting " board " instead of " minister", but in all these departments the minister is in charge.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: If the minister is in charge it removes that technical objection, but I do not see the Soldier Settlement Board mentioned anywhere in the bill. I now go back to the constitution of these committees. I would far rather see the machinery put simply and solely under the direction of the Soldier Settlement Board, which is qualified to handle it and which has competent officials already in its employ. In regard to these committees, how are you going to get satisfactory and responsible action from three provincial officials? I would suggest that that be fully considered in committee.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaksr, I wish to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Colonization to one of the clauses of the present act.
Subsection (c) of clause 2 defines crown lands as follows: "Crown lands", means any land suitable and available for settlement, lying within fifteen miles of a railway and owned by the Dominion government or any provincial government. In my county, Sir, there are three parishes inhabited by settlers who have established themselves on crown lands. These people have settled at a greater distance than fifteen miles from the railway, and, should the present legislation be adopted, according to the definition given to the term "crown lands," these settlers would be deprived of the benefits of the present act. I might add, by the way, that in the province of Quebec, if I be not mistaken, most of the settlers are established on lands located at a greater distance than fifteen miles from the railway. It, therefore, seems to me that should this legislation in its present form and as stated in Bill No. 16, carry, the province of 14011-136J
Quebec would be deprived of the benefits of this legislation.
I am aware that the west is ready to accept and admit that this distance of fifteen miles is sufficient; however, this limit must be further extended, if we wish this legislation to be beneficial to the settlers in the province of Quebec.
Again, I want to especially draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Colonization to this fact, and, I repeat it, if this bill is adopted in its present form, the province of Quebec will in no way benefit by it, and a number of settlers especially in my county, will be deprived of the benefits of this act.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I entirely agree with the statement made by the hon. member for Drummond and Arthabaska (Mr. Girouard). This measure would certainly be inoperative in the province of Quebec, should this fifteen miles limit, be included in this act.
I hafd no intention of discussing the matter on the second reading of the bill. I thought that we might look into this question when we were in committee. However, I deem it more loyal to warn the government and the hon. Minister of Colonization that this provision should necessarily disappear, if the act is to be applied throughout the country.
I think it may be stated that in the province of Quebec all the colonization districts lie, to-day-not in near-by settlements, but taken as a whole-at a greater distance than fifteen miles from the railway. This is true of the northern part of the county I represent, The same may be said for the county of Wright, Hull and, I think, for part of the county of Pontiac. The greater part of the lake St. John district which is available for settlement is more than fifteen miles distance from the railway. And precisely for the reason that, settlers who venture into the bush at a distance of 25, 30 or 40 miles from the railway, have greater difficulties to overcome than those who settle along railways, it seems to me that we should not say to them: "You shall get less encouragement than the others, because you have more pluck and spirit of enterprise."
On the other hand, I admit that when it is a question of colonization, in the province of Quebec or elsewhere, there has been far too much neglect, in the way of concentrating the inhabitants as was done with such good common sense 250 years ago under the French regime, and in inducing settlers to group together before thinking of spreading here and there through the bush and sometimes on
Advances to Settlers

lands little suited for farming. However, to establish an arbitrary ruling as the one which limits the operation of the act to 15 miles from the railway is not likely, in my opinion, to conduce to a very hearty reception of this measure, at least in the province of Quebec. I think the same may also be said for a large section of northern Ontario, where there are already centres for settlement which have been opened up at a greater distance than fifteen miles from the railway. I know nothing of the other provinces. That is to say, that I am not sufficiently acquainted with New Brunswick to know if there are settlers so located; but I would not be astonished if there were in certain sections of the interior of New Brunswick, settlers that are as much in need of assistance as the others, and whose farms are located more than fifteen miles away from the railway.
I do not intend to vote against the second reading of the bill; however, certainly if the bill is to remain as it is, I loyally warn the minister that I shall vote against the third reading.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: I would like to support the observations made by the member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Girouard) and by the member for Labelle (M;r. maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Before we proceed with
this bill I would like to ask the minister how he reconciles clause 4 with the pronouncement he made on Miarch 25 when the resolution preceding this bill was before the committee. At page 1887 of Hansard my hon. friend from Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) asked this question:

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS

Advances to Settlers

This-

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
No. The
provinces all have schemes of their own, but they are all interested in immigration. I cannot say whether the provinces will join in a scheme of this kind or not. My hon. friend knows that under the provisions of this bill the lands would have to be turned over to the federal government; at all events, the mortgage would be the first lien upon the provincial lands. The sole desire is to make this bill apply right across Canada in every province that is willing to come in under the scheme.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Then would it not be
proper to suggest to the minister that he should have consulted with the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec before the bill was brought down, for it is just as important that vacant lands in Ontario and in northern Quebec within the fifteen mile radius should be settled as vacant lands in any other province. The minister is himself suggesting under this scheme that no patent can be issued by the province of Quebec or the province of Ontario until the loan has been liquidated and the full amount returned to the Dominion government. This would suggest to me that the minister would have been in order if he had approached the governments of these two provinces, which, after all, are just as much interested in immigration and in the opening up of their back territories as any other province, as to what action they would take.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: One of the difficulties I have always found in connection with matters of this kind is that until you are able to speak definitely, you cannot make any arrangement with any province. I have tried it before in immigration matters. This is an attempt on the part of the government to treat all the provinces of Canada fairly and equitably, not debarring any of them. They are all interested in immigration and all have crown lands with the exception, I think, of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and they can all take advantage of this scheme if they so desire, but only, of course, if they are prepared to give the federal government the first mortgage upon the lands in question. That is why there are provisions in the act for dealing with provincial officials.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: The minister is perfectly aware there are only a few provinces in Canada that have any crown lands. The provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba have no crown lands.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Ah, the situation there is quite different.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Generally speaking the provinces which have crown lands are Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia, and, perhaps, New Brunswick. I understand the minister has made no attempt' to reach the authorities in these provinces in order to find out whether they will enter into a scheme of this kind or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
For the very good reason that I have, as yet, nothing definite that I can discuss with them. But when this bill has been passed I can do so. I am not sure that every one of the provinces will agree to give the federal government a priority of claim upon their lands. I anticipate that is one difficulty that will be encountered. But at the same time, all the provinces are more or less interested in the settlement of these vacant lands, and I am trying to get the consent of parliament to this bill in order that we may bring that about. Not only that, but the chief thing I am trying to accomplish through the medium of this bill is to hold out some hope to the Canadian who finds himself in an urban centre in this country and who is desirous of going back on the land without the investment of a great deal of

Advances to Settlers
money, of realizing that aim. That is the primary object I have in mind. The other object is to thicken up the settlement along the existing lines of railway. In discussing any matter of this kind even if you get one province to agree you have difficulty with another. That is the chief trouble in trying to devise any scheme applicable to the provinces as a whole.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Has there been any special demand for this legislation from any of the provinces outside of the three prairie provinces? As a matter of fact, we have in the province of Ontario, as the minister no doubt knows, what is called the Agricultural Development Board where loans are made to farmers at a low rate of interest and repaid in twenty annual instalments. Of course, in such cases they require to have the title which they do not here. At the moment I cannot conceive that there could be any demand for this legislation from the province of Ontario. If I felt the bill was going to be of any special benefit to that province I certainly would want to support it. I should therefore like to know from the minister, speaking to some extent for the province of Ontario, whether there has been any request from anybody in that province, either from the government or from individuals, calling for this legislation. Then comes the further question: Is it the purpose of this legislation to enable men to get advances of money if they have not security, or is it to enable them to secure loans when they have security? Prom what the minister has said, I should be inclined to think it is only when they have security that they can get such a loan. If that be the case why cannot they get money now? I can see, of course, one distinct advantage here, and that is in the rate of interest, and perhaps that is the main purpose of the legislation. If I am not putting too many questions at once, I should like the minister to give me information on that point also, because I do not suppose money can be got at five per cent in Ontario or Quebec or in the west-the interest rate in the west is probably seven or eight per cent, I think I am safe in saying that in the province of Ontario, unless you have what is called gilt-edge security, the rate of interest is 6J per cent. Therefore, there is a distinct advantage in getting an advance of money at five per cent. I am really more interested in the first question I put as to whether there has been any demand for this legislation from any province outside of the three prairie provinces, and if so from whom that demand 
has come? Is this an idea of the minister or of the department, or have there been persistent demands, perhaps extending over the last year or two, which have culminated in the bill before the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
There is a
fairly insistent demand from people who were residing in urban localities all over Canada that some scheme be devised which will afford them an opportunity to go back upon the land. I cannot say the demand comes from any particular section of Canada.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
May I interrupt the minister
at this point? Am I to understand that people in the city who are without means are seeking to go upon the land knowing they cannot get one dollar until they have made improvements to the value of $500 or $1,000 and then only to the extent of such improvements? Everybody knows that you must have money to make improvements, and you cannot get an advance under this bill until improvements have been made.	I cannot
really see that much good is going to resulfr from such a scheme as that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: My hon. friend will understand that the homesteading process is a pretty strenuous one, and the sole object in going upon a homestead is to avoid assuming a burden of debt. Otherwise no one would think of going on unimproved land. I am speaking in the light of experience. Now, there are in Canada-not altogether in the western part of the country, although there is a fairly large proportion there-people, farmers' sons for example, who have had agricultural experience. They have gone into cities and wish to return to the land but they find that the purchasing of improved land involves a heavy mortgage indebtedness. That is what they are anxious to avoid. There is always more or less opportunity for labour for such people in these localities where homestead land or crown land is available. They also have the opportunity of getting out and earning a little money in the older settled districts. You cannot hand three hundred or four hundred dollars to people and say to them "Go upon a given piece of land and earn that money." The chances are that in some cases they will be thoroughly honest about the transaction but as regards the remainder you will probably never see the money at all.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
The minister did not think
I was advocating such a thing as that, did he?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
No, I did
not. I am simply pointing out the difficulties

the department has to meet in trying to devise a satisfactory scheme in order to help the people referred to to go upon these lands. Some labour will be necessary before the lands become productive. The hope is to establish the settler on lands where he can put up a home out of the timber found upon the property-not sawn lumber but logs. He will also have to do some clearing. As he progresses with the construction of his buildings and his improvements, payments will be made, on progress estimates if you will, after inspection by officers of the Soldier Settlement Board. That is all that is involved in this.
I could not say that there has been any demand for it in Ontario or Quebec except that there comes generally to the department the request that something be done to assist people already in Canada to get back on the land. If this bill is not valuable for that purpose and also does not provide against exploitation of the government, I had better withdraw it. I am willing to have all the criticism offered that members of the committee feel like offering to the bill, but we must try, first, to preserve as far as possible the advances made by the government and, second, to render the maximum amount of assistance to people who are desirous of taking advantage of this measure. I do not deny that I expect a much larger proportion of people in the prairie provinces than in the older provinces of Canada to take advantage of it.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I think we may take
it for granted from what the minister has just said and also from the discussion which took place when this legislation was before the House in the form of a resolution, that the advantage, if any, to be derived from this bill will be felt chiefly, if not exclusively, in the three prairie provinces, and that the other provinces will be scarcely affected at all except as regards the amount of expenditure chargeable to the Dominion treasury in connection with carrying out this measure. I would be willing to assist in any settlement scheme which is going to produce results in any part of Canada, whether in the prairie provinces or in the other provinces, and if any reasonable result follows the expenditure of this money in the three prairie provinces I will feel well satisfied. So far as I can see this legislation will have little or no application to the other provinces.
Crown land as defined in the bill now before us, is land of the Dominion government or of a provincial government lying within fifteen miles of the railway and it must also be agricultural land. In Ontario any land
which would comply with that description and with those limitations would be in the far northern part of the province where I do not think we have a great quantity of agricultural land unless it be in what is known as the clay belt. That would be the only portion of Ontario that I think would be affected by the. operation of this measure. I do not know what portion of Quebec might be affected, but I would think also in that province the land would be pretty well to the north and land that would not in all probability be settled by agriculturists within the next five, ten, fifteen or twenty years. If, however, the passage of this measure and the making of these loans results in settlement of crown lands in the west under a system which affords proper safeguards to the Dominion of Canada so that the money will be eventually repaid, there may be some merit in the proposal and I for one would not like to oppose it because it may result in good.
The application of the clauses of this bill will be the all-important question. If this money is to be advanced by a suitable loan committee, by men of business experience, men who are actuated solely by a desire for the public weal apart from political considerations and the like, the matter may end well, but there is in this measure a tremendous opportunity to fall down in that very respect. Loose systems will be inaugurated; favouritism, political considerations and the like will creep in. I fear-and I express only my own fear-that in the result the money will not be repaid to the treasury of Canada. That has been our experience in a good many other instances in this country and I am afraid this $5,000,000 of expenditure which is the limit for any one year-
Mr. 'STEWART (Edmonton): It has been reduced to $1,000,000.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
-one million dollars will
be a matter of loss to the treasury in this way, that it will not be repaid, although if it should result- in securing for Canada any substantial volume of settlers I would not look upon it as actual loss to the country. I agree with the minister that the bill as drawn provides that an advance cannot be made except upon improvements actually effected and I see the difficulty which the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys) has pointed out. How is a man who has no money to make the initial improvements in order to get a loan? The difficulty is going to be to find the man who has the money to go on the land and make the first improvements because, if the improvements are to be such as to afford reasonable security, the

Advances to Settlers
settler must in the first instance have some substantial amount to put into the undertaking. Once you have the man on the land with the improvements your scheme may work well, but how you are going to get the initial improvements as security for advances out of this fund, it is hard for one to know.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
We anight just as well be
frank about this matter in commencing, and admit that this scheme will apply more particularly to the prairie provinces than to the other provinces of the Dominion, for the simple reason that the prairie provinces have more land of the character that this legislation will be applicable to. We may take a too restricted view of the matter and the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) touched upon it when he spoke of the benefit it would be to the country at large. I am inclined to believe if you can get settlers to go on this land and improve it the country as a whole will benefit more than those settlers.
As regards want of money to begin with, strange as it may seem those of us who were acquainted with conditions that prevailed in the early settlement of the prairie provinces- and I think the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) knows something about this-know that a great number of homesteads were taken up by people who had just enough money to pay ithe original ten dollars. Yet when I look back over those years and I think of the people who have made good in western Canada, I find in the great majority of cases the people who made good were those verj ones who, to commence with, had only a ten dollar stake in the land they took up. Therefore the fact that a man has no money should not stand in the way. There are always many opportunities for men to obtain employment in the west at good wages; for notwithstanding all that we hear about the lack of work, the demand at the present time for men on the farms cannot ibe filled. That demand always exists, and there is no doubt that any man who is willing to work hard and to adapt himself to his surroundings can advance his material interests by going on the land. He may not find everything precisely to his liking on the farm, but if he is prepared1 to put up with a little hardship he can easily make a home for himself by taking advantage of the conditions offered in this bill.
I have received letters from people of foreign birth who have some doubt as to whether they will come under the provisions of the bill. As I understand the legislation,
I think they will. It is being provided that

" Canadian citizen " shall be defined by the Immigration Act. It seems to me that when *a man has become a Canadian citizen under that act he will automatically become eligible to take advantage of the provisions of this bill. I am not so sanguine as the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) about the great work that will be accomplished. I do not think that you will see vast sums of money spent under this legislation, but it is undoubtedly worthy of a trial. I believe, further, that a great majority of the people who will take advantage of it will be either those of foreign birth or the children of foreign parentage. They are the ones who are willing to adjust themselves to the conditions of agricultural life. They are willing to endure more hardship and to make a more vigorous struggle than our own Canadians are likely to undertake. As a matter of fact I question whether the average Canadian of today is really an agriculturist; he looks more to business and to the professions. I am sorry that this is so, but I am afraid that we shall see the same thing take place in western Canada that occurred in the northwestern states; unless there is a change the great bulk of our agricultural people-that is to say, the people who will make a success of farming

will be people of foreign birth or parentage. I sincerely hope this will not foe the case. My own effort has been to elevate as far as possible the whole calling of .agriculture. For that reason I am in favour of the bill inasmuch as in my opinion it will work out to the advantage of the prairie provinces.
I have no jealousy towards any of the other provinces in regard to this legislation. As a matter of fact, as I have said before, anything that will help western Canada to become settled and to make production possible must react to the benefit of the Dominion as a whole. And conditions in the west lend themselves to a bill of this kind to a greater degree than do' the conditions in other parts of Canada.
In regard to the fifteen mile limit, I do not know whether anything can be done in relation to Quebec or Ontario, but certainly I am in favour of that provision for the west. At the same time it is possible that something-might be done in the way of regulation to extend a further limit, if necessary, to the other provinces. On the whole I firmly believe that the bill is a wise one so far as western Canada goes, and I am prepared to. vote for it.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I just want to amplify
what I said before in regard to the province.

Advances to Settlers
of Quebec. It would be a mistake to suppose that the inhabitants of that province are not going back to the land at all. We have been carrying on an intensive campaign through the clergy, the press, and our colonization societies and have obtained splendid results. One has only to look at the northern part of Quebec along the Transcontinental railway where the Abitibi settlement has sprung up in the last fifteen years. The district is now represented in the local legislature and in parliament, and it has full judicial machinery. There are now twenty parishes in the settlement, and the clergy look to the future of the district with great hopes. The same thing might be said of the lake St. John district. No part of Canada is at present attracting more attention that that district, which is becoming a magnet of interest to the whole world. A new city is springing up there known as Arvida, where aluminum works, water-power and pulp mills will operate. In the lake St. John district, which is many miles from any railway, a most extraordinary settlement is going on; and the same is true, although to a lesser degree, of the counties of Labelle, Wright and the northern part of Joliette, of Montcalm, and of the region beyond Three Rivers, down into the Gaspe territory. We are opening up at the present time in the Gaspe peninsula, in the counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe, a number of parishes half way between the St. Lawrence and the baie des Chaleurs anywhere from fifteen to twenty-five miles removed from old settlements. I should therefore like to see the province of Quebec take advantage of the benefits of this legislation. We should not leave the country to imagine that only the west will be opened up for settlement.
I can understand the arbitrary limit of fifteen miles being fixed for the prairies, but as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) pointed out on a former occasion, we have changed our system of settlement in the province of Quebec from what it was under the French regime. Under the French regime the original immigrants settled along the waterways, which were then practically the sole means of communication. Now, however, they have gone considerable distances inland, so that we have in the province parishes thirty, forty and fifty miles from a railway. Those parishes are fully organized and the impression prevails to-day, as it has prevailed during a number of years past, that the province through its legislature will be forced by public opinion to undertake some such scheme as this as a means of encouraging the people to return to the land.
We all know that the salvation of Canada lies in a more even distribution of its population as between city and country. If the majority of our people continue to live in cities and urban settlements, I do not know what is going to become of the country in the next generation or two. It seems to me that every possible effort should be made to induce the people to go back to the land. If the minister must of necessity fix an arbitrary limit for the west, I urge him to leave the question open, at least so far as Quebec is concerned, until negotiations can be carried on with the provincial government.
I am sure that the people of the province of Quebec are anxious to take hold of this scheme because the desire there is to have settlers come in. The people of Quebec will go into parts of the country where the immigrant from Europe or from the British Isles will not go. They are typical woodsmen who are quite prepared to settle in the northern parts of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, just as the pioneers in those provinces did long ago. I do not think, therefore, that they should be debarred from the benefits of this legislation by any provision compelling them to settle within fifteen miles of communication; the localities that are thus accessible are already settled. In order to have new settlements we must go beyond that limit.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I rise merely to confirm
in part what the last speaker (Mr. Marcil) said. I am opposed to this bill for the reason that it is purely local in its application, being confined to western Canada, and my opinion has been Confirmed by the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke), who states quite frankly that he believes that the benefits, if any, will accrue only to that part of the country. There are large territories, both in Ontario and in Quebec, where there are settlers to whom a loan of a thousand or even five hundred dollars would be a decided boon. Those settlers are anxious to remain on the land with their families, and as the hon. member (Mr. Marcil) has well said, they are the best pioneers in the world to-day. They are opening up an empire in the northern part of Ontario and Quebec, and in my opinion this bill, if it is to be effective, should be the subject of negotiation between the minister and the provincial governments who have crown lands of their own. Only on that basis should the legislation be adopted.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to encourage colonization through the lending of money at a low rate of interest. I think it might go further and extend to all land
Advances to Settlers

within the Dominion. In other words, you are building up at one end by encouraging people to come here, and you are tearing down at the other end by not recognizing those who are already on the land. In that connection I want to cite a very interesting case which was brought to my attention no later than March 20. It is contained in a letter written to me by a man who is a farmer and a member of a farmers institute, so it is evident that he takes an interest in agricultural affairs. We have in British Columbia a Land Settlement Board which is supposed to make advances to and encourage men on the land. We have also the Soldier Settlement Board, a federal institution. So this man had an opportunity to apply to the two boards. He writes:
I have tried the two local establishments, the Soldier Settlement Board and the Land Settlement Board, to raise a loan on my ranch. I thought that the Land Settlement Board were going to advance the money, but at the final stage they decided that as the money was not to be used for new improvements they would not make the advance.
In other words, you are going to lend money to a new settler as he makes his improvements; but the collateral is not considered good enough for improvements that have already been made. This man adds that he has a clear' title to thirty acres, has constructed a five-roomed house, a barn, root houses, cellars, and so on. He writes:
It is my own home, the only one I have, and I want to raise $1,000. I had ten weeks with pneumonia.
Now, you are going to encourage newcomers, but here is a man who has cleared thirty acres, built a house and barn and gone through various trials and hardships. He considers that his ten weeks' illness put him back two years. Worse still, just before recovering he broke three ribs. But that is not the most serious part of his troubles. He goes on:
We had our children sick, two operations in the hospital, and what with doctors bills, and so on, I am about $850 behind.
By this legislation you are inviting men from the city to go on the land, but you are not offering any encouragement to those who are already there. This unfortunate man says:
I am in danger of losing what I have, and after four years and eight months overseas to come back and put every cent I had into a ranch, and then lose it.
You are not doing anything for this man who has put in four years and eight months overseas, but you are inviting some chap from the city or some outsider to go on the land and make improvements, for which you are quite willing to advance him money. These loans should be available to bona fide settlers, the men who by their energies have 
cleared their land and put up buildings; but you are not disposed to consider them at all.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Would not the case mentioned by the hon. member be a proper one for a rural credit scheme?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
No matter what might be
the proper scheme, the fact remains that in British Columbia both the Land Settlement Board and the Soldier Settlement Board are overlooking such a case as this, and if this is not a worthy case I do not know what is. Certainly in my view no worthier case could come before any settlement board. Let me cite a similar case. Twenty miles north of Bassano which is eighty miles east of Calgary, a man purchased 160 acres. He paid So00 in cash. He and his family moved on to the land, fenced and broke 80 acres and seeded it. Unfortunately, the first year they did not get a crop. The next year that man came and asked me as a favour if I would write to the government at Edmonton to see if some arrangement could not be made to give him sufficient seed. The reply came back that nothing could be done. What was the result? The man simply abandoned his place and he and the three members of his family went over to the States. What is the good of encouraging people to come into this country if you are not going to take care of those already here?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
What year
was that?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
In the spring of 1924. I
applied to the department at Edmonton for some relief for the man by way of seed. I submit that it is of far greater importance to take care of the people who are already here than to bring in outsiders.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to place myself on record as being absolutely opposed to this measure. As a western representative I cannot agree to anything like this proposal

to take a man out of the city and give him SI ,000 or to give a new settler $500 to go on the land. We have had those spoon-fed babies in western Canada and we know something about them. Really I cannot understand the minister bringing in such a bill. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) knows something about conditions close to where he lives. If this measure is passed I can see that the treasury will be exploited, and the security taken for the loans advanced will be practically nil. Take the log house and a few other buildings that a man puts up on his land, they look fairly well, and your inspector comes along and authorizes a loaD

Advances to Settlers
of $1,000; but that man comes from the city, he is not a success on the land, and finally the government will own it. I cannot understand the minister sponsoring this bill knowing western Canada as he does. It may be all right for Quebec-I do not know what the conditions are there-but let Quebec be responsible for part of the commitment. Such a measure may be all right to help settlers in that province, but so far as western Canada is concerned, I would urge the government to do something to help the man on the land get his products to the markets of the world. Then we will have no trouble in getting settlers there.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I rise to a point of order,
Mr. Chairman. This discussion I submit is entirely out of order. We are dealing with the first section of the bill, its title, and it is a well known fact that in committee of the whole the principle of a bill cannot be discussed; that should be dealt with on the second reading. I think we will really get along much quicker if we discuss the various sections as we come to them instead of making general observations dealing with the whole bill.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: What the hon. member says is strictly true, but I never yet saw the rule enforced, and I do not know how in the world it could be.

cannot enforce the rule of not discussing the principle of the bill.

speechtext: But the principle comes into everything, and usually any attempt to enforce the rule takes up more time than would be consumed by the discussion on the bill itself. The objection I have to this bill is that it is no good. There are objections in detail to this clause and that, but what in the world the bill is here for I cannot understand. The member for Brandon says that he supports the bill. We all know that; if he did not the bill would not be here, we would never have had it introduced.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I might remind the right
hon. leader of the opposition that he assumes to know everything that I know.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
It is another tribute to the honesty of the hon. member that he did not deny it. Take the whole of Canada into account; this bill is to be paid for and all the money has to be provided by the whole
Dominion. Leave out the three prairie provinces in the meantime, and you have six provinces left. Can anyone give me any suggestion of a reason why we should plunge into the arena and offer our money by millions to these six provinces? They are not asking for it; some of them have no crown lands at all. To those who have none, it is a joke to think of their coming in under this bill; their only privilege would be to contribute to the raising of the money. That is all they will get, but in the other provinces which have crown lands, the onus and responsibility for their settlement is solely provincial. That responsibility they are discharging and they are not asking our help. Why then should we address ourselves to them and say, "You do not know how to settle your crown lands. Here is some of the overflowing treasury of Canada; take that and see if you cannot do a little better." Is that not what we are really doing under this measure? Is the treasury of Canada so flush; is the ocean so full that we have to find- new channels into which to divert it?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Was not that done in 1919 and 1920, when the highways were built?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Those were equally applicable to the other provinces; there was not any difference in that regard. The whole Dominion is interested in highways, for the reason that the people of one province traverse the highways of another; the people of Quebec are interested in the highways of Ontario and the people of Ontario are interested in the highways of Quebec. Even at that, many a bill has been introduced in this House with more justification than the highways bill of that time, and while I think the grounds were a thousand times stronger than in the present case, the experience of the highways measure was such as to warn us against transgressing even in a case so favourable as this. But here Ontario is not asking for this measure; New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are surely not asking for more burdens, and that is what this measure brings. Is the cry from the west so plaintive and so appealing that we must do injustice to all the other provinces in order to plunge there and try to get more money out on loans? I do not think it is.
Let us consider the bill as it applies to the west. It covers homestead lands at present unoccupied, crown lands within fifteen miles of a railway. In the west it would be more objectionable if it went beyond the fifteen miles-that I admit; so we need not discuss the area beyond that limit. Let us take the
Advances to Settlers

area within fifteen miles of a railway. It is open to homesteading now and has been open to homesteaders for, I should say, thirty years and probably longer. Not a man has gone on that land, or anyone who has gone on has abandoned it as a failure. What is the general presumption as to the character of that land? The general presumption, even on the part of those who do not know it and have not been over the territory, is that it is not good farming land or it would be occupied to-day by men who can get an entry for $10 and have only to make very, very moderate improvements for three years in order to get title to 160 acres. I know from my experience as Minister of the Interior that every quarter section of land that was farmable at all and a fit home for a settler, within fifteen miles of a railway, was continually in demand. I was called upon as the officers of the department were called upon time and again, to pass upon the claims of this man and that man. Many a time those claims were for land not worth farming. Now we are trying to bring in a high pressure policy, to force people to buy these lands as farm lands. Is it wise? We say to them, "We will give you money at 5 per cent interest; we will take it out of the treasury and make the other provinces contribute in order to see if we cannot get someone on that land, to make a farm out of it." I do not see any national object to be served. As a matter of fact you are not going to help that settler; you are going to get him into debt on a bad farm, and if there is any place in perdition worse than that I do not know where it is. Let me repeat; you are going to get the settler into debt on a poor farm.
We have any amount of good land in western Canada; a great deal of it is occupied, and what is not occupied is pretty far from the railway. The objective of parliament should be to create a market for the products of the farm, so that a man on a good farm can make it go. No man on a poor farm can make a success of it; I do not think I have ever known of an exception to that statement. This land, as a rule, is bad land. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) says, "You are going to help the country more than you will help the settler." I would like to ask this committee how we are going to help the country if we do not help the settler. If by lending a settler public money you do not help him, in what imaginable way can you help the country? You cannot do it. You will only get the country into more debt and the settlers in debt, in turn, to the country-a debt which I venture to say at this distance of time will, 
in the great majority of cases, never be repaid.
The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) argues against this bill in the province of Quebec. By the way, how is it that when the hon. member is criticizing this government he always speaks in French, and when he is supporting it he always speaks in English? I would like very much if he would reverse the process. In so doing we would have a great many more French speeches by him and the educational effect of his speeches in this House would be much greater. I think, really, that that is the best effect his speeches have, at any rate those made in support of the government. The hon. member criticizes this bill on the ground that it will not apply to the province of Quebec because of the fifteen mile limit. For the very same reason it cannot apply to the western provinces, because within the fifteen mile limit the amount of land which men ought to try to farm is so limited that there is no call for the bill at all.
I suggest to the minister that he simplify the whole problem by giving the bill up. Let him add it to the long list of rejected statutory misfits which this government has introduced; add it to the Platinum bill; the Petersen contract; the single transferable vote, and I do not know how many others; add it to the long, long array of abandoned, deserted children of the administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I am very
glad, Mr. Chairman, to see my right hon. friend so facetious this afternoon, and I am also glad to see that he has such a wide knowledge of western homestead conditions. I take issue, however, with my hon. friend on a few points which he mentioned. I am willing to grant my hon. friend the wide realm of knowledge which he has exposed to the committee this afternoon; I am ready to admit that this government, as well as my hon. friend's government, have introduced legislation which has received severe criticism at the hands of members of this House; it might well he said that a very great deal of the legislation introduced by my hon. friend could be subjected to very severe criticism. But when he makes the statement that in western Canada there is no good agricultural land within fifteen miles of the existing railways, my hon. friend is very wide of the mark indeed. He might again visit western Canada and thereby increase his knowledge of conditions as they actually exist.
What is the outstanding difficulty, in western Canada and elsewhere? Is it not that we are entirely over-built with railways? Who is

Advances to Settlers
responsible for that, may I ask my hon. friend? I do not name any particular government, but he will have to take his share of the responsibility, as will everyone else.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Not guilty.
M.\ STEWART (Edmonton):	My hon.
friend need not say that; the government of which he was a member is just as guilty as any other government, and to just as great a degree. We have this situation on our hands, and when my hon. friend says that these lands would have been taken up long ago if they had been of any value, he is again very wide of the mark. These lands have been passed up primarily for the reason that they are difficult to clear, and my hon. friend is quite right when he says that he as well as myself has been appealed to time and again for the purpose of easing up on the provisions so as to allow a man to earn a patent on these lands. For what purpose- for the purpose of getting a loan in order to let that man get on the land. That is the history of homesteading as I know it and as my hon. friend knows it, if he will only cast his mind back over his administration. Invariably when these loans are put on the land, they carry a rate of eight per cent interest, and sometimes more. The sole object of this legislation is to assist the settler who has the courage and the endurance to tackle this kind of land. May I say to my hon. friend that there is a very considerable area of lands within the fifteen mile radius in western Canada that are just as good as any land in western Canada that is now under agricultural development, and it was with the thought of assisting in their development that this bill has been brought down. If it is of no use to meet a situation of that kind, if it is wise to leave these lands that are within a reasonable distance of existing railways vacant and to put a badge of inferiority on them, just let them remain as they are and haul the tonnage past these lands, all right; we need do nothing about it. But my thought was otherwise. My object has always been to create intensive settlement, not to scatter it. I have frequently said in Alberta that if someone had put a fence across the province at the city of Edmonton and prevented people from going into northern Alberta our problems in that province would have been reduced a thousandfold, and probably that applies to every western province.
My hon. friend says that in the discussion of this bill we connot confine ourselves to the sections under discussion. Neither can I confine settlement. Wherever there is open land available for settlement, whether it is ten or
twenty or fifty or one hundred miles from a railway, invariably you will find settlers flocking into that locality. Then we have demands for the building of roads and railways, and all that is incidental thereto.
These lands have been inspected by the Soldier Settlement Board-I am speaking now entirely of the three western provinces-and the board informs me that there is a very considerable area of these lands within fifteen miles of existing railways which have been inspected by them and which will warrant settlement, and warrant advances as settlement proceeds. Rather than have the settler struggle along for two or three years and become, in many cases, discouraged and leave his land, the hope was that with this meagre assistance -it is meagre, and at a low rate of interest as pointed out by the hon. member for North Simcoe-settlement would be encouraged. But if this assistance will be of no help to the settler, then we had better abandon the whole project, and leave the lands, as my hon. friend has designated them, as lands that are unfit for settlement. But I do not agree with him. Profiting from the experience the Soldier Settlement Board have gained in recent years in settling lands that were improved, I think we shall not have the large number of mistakes that were made in the past, perhaps in consequence of more immature knowledge with respect to settlement, and I think the bill will serve a very useful purpose.
With respect to the older provinces, there is no desire to interfere with their settlement. The claim has been frequently made in eastern Canada that this government does nothing, as previous governments did nothing, to assist in the settlement of the older provinces or to keep people there. As a matter of fact, there is a general demand from the older provinces that the federal government assist them to get more settlement; in Nova Scotia, for instance. I notice my hon. friends in the back benches appear to applaud those who opposed this bill. In the province of Nova Scotia there is an active demand that we procure settlers for them. For what purpose? Primarily to settle upon abandoned lands. There does not seem to be any particular demand for labour in those provinces, and that is the demand we get from them, and we have arranged with the government of Nova Scotia to bring in boys, whom they undertake to settle. The governments in the older provinces I am well aware are trying to settle their crown lands, and are making loans upon them. It is true that very few provincial governments are making loans on improved lands in western Canada, with the exception of Saskatchewan, but in British Columbia,
Advances to Settlers

Ontario and Quebec, they are all doing something to try and settle their crown lands. In all probability the fifteen mile limit would be a bar in the case of the older provinces, but I am convinced, as is the leader of the opposition, that we should not go beyond the fifteen mile limit in western Canada.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
When this matter
came up by way of resolution in committee, I mentioned some phases of this bill in regard to which I	havp not	as	yet received anysatisfactory explanation. If Manitoba can be benefitted by this legislation, the constituency I represent	may also	be	benefitted	by it.Whenever immigration or settlement is discussed in this House it seems to be taken for granted that the expenditure will be made for western	Canada alone.	I would	like toremind the	committee	that in 1924,	of the90.000	odd immigrants who came to Canada,40.000	stayed in Ontario, and 15,000 in Quebec, so I do not see why it should be taken for granted that only western Canada will necessarily benefit from a colonization scheme, though people of discretion will probably go to the west. Moreover, the government has probably a greater responsibility in connection with western lands, because they still have control of the crown lands.
The suggestion has been made that this legislation could not benefit the settler because he must first make his improvements before he could get a loan. I disagree wholly with that view. If a man who is fitted to go on the land and settle knows he can get a loan when improvements have been made he will be able to find means of staying on the land, and if the land is adequate security for the loan, I would not oppose it on that ground at all. I can conceive of substantial good being done if it is possible for people to get loans as part of a colonization scheme, but the making of loans to individuals is not the government's responsibility, because they should not encourage people to go on the lands who cannot, under the conditions I am going to detail, make a success of farming, either for lack of money or because of certain mental and physical characteristics. The reason lands within fifteen miles of a railway in Manitoba have not been settled in the past is this: By virtue of their not having obtained patents municipal organization has been impossible and without it the settlers cannot do the very things that are essential to make settlement a success. This is the fundamental mistake the government has always made in colonization. They put on these lands people with nothing, or next to nothing, and they

have no capacity by municipal organization to raise the money that is absolutely necessary to provide adequate roads and the drainage that is necessary. A man can work as hard as he likes and then come back to his farm, but that land is going to remain unproductive and he cannot make any headway if there is no municipal organization to provide the essential things the settlement needs. Settlements were made twenty years ago between the lakes. They tried or organize municipalities, and they are now disorganized. The settlers have not been able to make a success, not because they were unwilling to hew down the timber and clear the land, but because, having no municipal organization, they could get no drainage and no roads. Many have abandoned these lands, and unless the government realizes its responsibility in this respect, settlement on these heavy timbered lands, which are generally wet too, will not be a success, and so in connection with any assistance of the kind detailed in this bill the government should provide, as was done away back in the seventies and eighties, for a certain amount of drainage and road building to make settlement possible. Then. I maintain, these people will not need loans, or they will be able to get loans from private sources. That is why I asked the minister whether he was going to make any provision for a priority of municipal taxation, or whether he was prepared to give any undertaking that the taxes would be paid by the settler concurrently with the interest on the loan, and in the event of failure by that settler and the government having to take back the land, whether they would recognize the lien for taxes when they did so. I think these two provisions ought to be inserted in the bill because if you do not make municipal machinery and municipal work possible you are going to create an added difficulty for struggling municipalities so many of which have become disorganized in the last few years and in rvhich the settlers have abandoned their lands. There is one other question I should like to ask and it is this: If the bill carries, would the settler who is now on crown land for which he has not received a patent be entitled to come under the act, and will the taxes created in respect to such lands have priority over the government loan that is now proposed ?
