maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Coming from one of the large
rural constituencies in the province of Manitoba, I wish to place myself on record with respect to this bill,1 In my opinion the measure will not help very materially to settle vacant lands within fifteen miles of a railway in Manitoba for the reasons pointed out by previous speakers. Those who wish to take advantage of the provisions of the bill first have to establish themselves on the land at their own expense, and afterwards make application to the government for a loan. I agree with the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) that the security for such loans granted to the settlers will be practically worthless. We know that from experience. Those of us who have had experience in pioneering conditions, in Ontario and Quebec as well as in western Canada, know that the men who make good on the land are those who go there on their own initiative. I do not think the present scheme is practicable. I have heard the claim made during this discussion that the western provinces will
Advances lo Settlers

benefit from the proposed' legislation to a greater degree than the other provinces of the Dominion. Speaking for the province oi Manitoba, if I may be allowed to do so, I do not think it has made any demand for such legislation at the present time. That is my opinion. At any rate I have not heard any such demand from my people in Manitoba. I believe the bill will involve an added liability to the Dominion, and at the same time will not help this country to any material extent. Consequently I join in the opinion which has been expressed by other speakers that the bill might very well be dropped for the present.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I may say that I am in
favour of the bill. I was somewhat disappointed to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hay) and also the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins). I am not surprised at the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition. I think he has been so long detached from western Canada, and from the conditions there, that he has lost touch with questions of this kind. I stand squarely behind this legislation. A number of hon. members who have spoken have failed to appreciate the difference between the possibilities of settling on a homestead or a new location to-day and those which existed twenty years ago. I venture to say there is not a member in this House from western Canada who homesteaded, say twenty or twenty-five years ago, who will stand up here and say that he would not regard with some fear the possible success he might experience in attempting to homestead under the conditions which prevail at this time. It is impossible for anyone without any money to homestead at this time such lands as are available in western Canada and that is the reason why our people are not homesteading. It is easy for hon. members to stand up in their places in this House and talk about what they did twenty-five years ago. I homesteaded twenty-five, twenty-six or twenty-seven years ago and I know many others who homesteaded about that time and were successful, but I would not attempt to homestead to-day without any money and in the belief that I would be successful. It "can't be did "-that is all. The standards of twenty-five years ago are not the standards of today. When I homesteaded, if I had a good suit of overalls I thought I was pretty lucky. That is not the case to-day. In those days you could purchase lumber for ten dollars a thousand; to-day it costs about sixty or sixty-five dollars a thousand, and other things cost in proportion. It is unfair to expect a

new settler to go back to the standards of thirty or forty years ago.
This legislation is the first approach to anything tangible in the direction of a real settlement scheme. Australia is spending money by the hundreds of millions on settlement. It has been my privilege to discuss the question of land settlement in Australia with members of the Australian government and they tell me it is the finest scheme that has ever been introduced into that country. They have almost to build fences around Australia to keep the people out. We must spend money if we are going to get settlers on the land. I hope this bill passes because it will be a real boon not only to the western provinces but to many other parts of Canada. I am sure any hon. member who has travelled through western Canada and has seen the millions of acres of good land lying along our railways with no settlers on it must be impressed with the necessity of putting people on that land in order to furnish traffic for the railways running through those areas. In fact, I would have favoured a more extensive scheme and I am sorry the amount has been reduced to S1,000,0G0. section of northern Ontario, that gap between North Bay and the Manitoba boundary, which has an area as great as the countries of Germany and France combined and yet which has a population of, perhaps, a couple of hundred thousand people. It contains hundreds of thousands of acres of good agricultural land when it is cleared. It is bush land, land which the good French-Canadian people love to settle upon and which many people in Europe would be glad to settle upon. It is an immense gap extending for some 700 miles between North Bay and the Manitoba boundary where the railways do not get the traffic they should, across which three railways run, and which should be built up if at all possible to provide traffic for those railways in that section where railway traffic is most scarce. That applies also to the northern sections of Quebec. I believe in such questions as this we should bring in bills more applicable to the whole of the Dominion than just, as the minister pointed out himself, to the prairie provinces. He mentioned earlier in his remarks this afternoon that he had not consulted with Ontario or Quebec or the other provinces. He said that he wanted to get this legislation through, to have this bill pass the House, and then he would consult with the other provinces. Might I ask this honourable House if that is the time to consult with Ontario, Quebec, the Maritimes and British Columbia as to bringing about settlement which will apply to them as well? I would suggest to the minister that the time to consult with Ontario, Quebec and the other provinces, outside of the prairie provinces which are directly affected by this legislation, is before the bill becomes law and not after, and I make the suggestion, with the best of intentions and with no politics back of it, that this bill should be held up; that the minister should consult with Ontario, Quebec, the Maritimes and British Columbia as well as the prairie provinces, of course, and get their ideas upon some form of a bill which, when brought in, will help to settle those vast lands of northern Ontario and Quebec, which will help to bring back settlers into those lands in the Maritimes and in British Columbia as well as in the prairie provinces. I do not think it is fair to the rest of this country that on nearly all occasions the other provinces should be asked simply to foot bills the effect of which is to settle people only in the prairie provinces. I suggest in all sincerity to the minister that he should hold up this bill, consult with the other provinces affected, and endeavour to bring in a bill

which will be satisfactory to all sections of this country instead of merely to the prairie provinces, and apparently the present legislation is not very satisfactory to them if we are to judge by the speeches which we have heard from all parts of this House to-day.

speechtext:
I want to say a word on two phases of the question before the House. First I desire to support what has been said by my hon. friend (Mr. Manion). Listening to the discussions in this House, one would fancy that there were no agricultural lands left in any part of Canada except the prairies; but anyone who knows anything about Quebec and Ontario knows exactly what my hon. friend has pointed out, namely, that there are hundreds of thousands of acres of the very best agricultural land waiting for settlement in the northern parts of those two provinces. At this point let me say that if in working out schemes of this character something were done for the lands referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Mullins), similar to what has been done in northern Ontario and northern Quebec, where the governments, by means of the construction of highways and through drainage on a large scale, before the settler goes on the land, have spent their money to open up the country and make it accessible to men desiring to settle, people would much more readily take up agriculture. I make that general observation in passing.
Coming to the principle of the legislation- I understand we are discussing the preamble to the bill-I want to ask the government how many of these schemes are going to be presented to parliament. When the estimates were brought down some time ago considerable noise was made about the saving that was being effected this year in comparison with last year. Have all these schemes, involving the expenditure of millions of dollars, been taken into consideration in the preparation of those estimates? This is just one bill; there are several others to be dealt with, one with regard to old age pensions, which will entail an expenditure of twenty or twenty-five million dollars, another with relation to rural credits, others in regard to railways, and so forth. These various proposals are to be submitted to parliament, and the haphazard manner in which they are being introduced, as my hon. friend from Fort William has suggested, is evidenced in this very discussion to-day. The minister, after preparing this bill himself, does not know apparently how much money he really requires. On a former occasion he informed the House that he wanted $5,000,000 to carry out the proposals of the bill, but to-day he finds that he 
requires only $1,000,000. How did the minister arrive at that estimate of $5,000,000, when he can be persuaded to reduce it now to $1,000,000? Does not this very fact suggest that we should pause to consider the direction in which we are travelling in the matter of these expenditures? The purpose for which the last, parliament was dissolved and an election held, if the Prime Minister's words mean anything, was that the peoples' representatives might deal with such outstanding problems as railway transportation, taxation and questions of equal importance. And this is the way in which we are dealing with those great problems: we are solving them by bringing in slipshod measures to which mature consideration has not been given,-measures that will mean an addition to the burden of debt under which the people of the Dominion are-now suffering.

Both the minister's
former speech and the present one are intended to convince the committee that there is a field for the application of the bill in what are known as the scrub lands of the west, lands that are hard to cultivate and hard and very expensive to bring into a state in which cultivation is possible. I am afraid the minister has not convinced me. I do not think there are lands in quantity within 15 miles of a railway which are not either so heavily scrubbed as to be valueless for homesteading or for some other reason are not security for $500 or $1,000. In the first place, neither $.500 nor even $1,000 will go very far towards clearing these lands. The minister may get his man on the land and leave him to put the $500 of his mortgage to this purpose or that. But when he goes back next year he will find the scrub there still and the mortgage on it, too, and it will be a pretty scrubby mortgage. The minister will find that he will lose this money. I speak rather feelingly on the subject because I have had some experience myself. You cannot get those lands cultivated by a system of government subvention. I will put the case in a nut shell this way: Do not try to help the settler by helping him into debt; help him to get out of it. If you get more people into the district, then it will be far better to sell the land at $1 an acre or anything you can get for it at auction; for the man who buys it will have to see that is cultivated pretty soon or his taxes will eat him out of house and home. If you get people into the district, then the economic conditions will invite cultivation of land like that; but to try to force cultivation in advance by government loans means loss of money, and it does not get settlement. .The minister knows as well as I do that in western Canada, in Ontario even-I doubt not in. Quebec, although that is likely there; certainly in the Maritime provinces-there are large acreages of abandoned land now, and a lot of it is pretty good land. I have seen in Prince Edward Island just about as nice a farm as one would want to live on, abandoned, the farmer gone. There are doubtless several reasons for it; but in the face of that situation, with land privately owned that can be bought for almost nothing, how can you justify taxing those people in order to force a premature cultivation of heavily scrubbed land in the west? And especially how can you justify taxing the owners of land in western Canada-of fairly good land which cannot be made to pay even to-day; at least you cannot get people on
Advances to Settlers

it-how can you justify taxing those people in order to force new land under cultivation?
Now, I know Saskatchewan and Alberta have not been invaded by the modern weed quite to the degree that Manitoba has, but it is moving in that direction, and instead of seeking to force virgin land under the plough by this piece of legislation and that, by this subvention and that, it would be far better to intensify work on the land already under cultivation-and there is far more of it under cultivation today than we are getting results from-I say. it would be far better to intensify cultivation on that land and by assistance restrict the inroads of these weed pests. The more land you bring under cultivation the harder that problem is.
I do not believe in trying to anticipate the future, in trying to get more and more land here, there and everywhere under the plough. As a matter of fact what good is it going to do the farmer to get more farmers there? Get people to use the farmer's products, and you help him. How is it we are exerting ourselves so much to get somebody else to produce more grain?. Everybody seems to agree-some on this side of the House-that we ought to concentrate on getting more people on the land. Well, I never had any sympathy with that view at all. I want to get more people of all occupations into this country. From the standpoint of the farmer, the more people you get in other occupations and the fewer in his the better for him. You are not helping the farmer by adding to his competition, while at the same time those who consume his products are dwindling. I do not believe in this special legislation to coax, cajole, bribe people to go on the land. They will go on the land if you make conditions such that it will pay them. We will make the land pay by our policies, which would add ta the population of the country. Now, there may be other policies aside from those which we habitually press upon this House; doubtless there are. But one of our policies is not to take hundreds of thousands of dollars out of the treasury to force into premature cultivation lands that are not needed to be under cultivation at all, because of the great excess of lands that are already under cultivation. Scores of thousands of acres of land, even in our western country, have already been rescued from the scrub; millions of dollars have been spent to bring the land into that condition, yet to-day it is not half cultivated. This is still more true, let me repeat, of the older provinces. Under these circumstances it surely is not a wise policy, it certainly is not an economic policy, to be making provision at this time of day in our legislation for

We have heard many

I cannot speak with the authority of antiquity which my hon. friend can command, but I never heard of it before. I know there was assistance given on the principle of a reward to the soldiers, especially those who came to this country during the war of 1812 and who wished to stay, but. we are now told that there was a system of loans on lands for the purpose of settlement, made by the British government. If there was such I must frankly admit that I have never heard of it. In the district from which I come, which is some distance from the district of the minister, there was a system of loans by the Canada Company-I think that was the title of the company-but I do not know of any relationship between that company and the British government. From that company the settlers of western Ontario obtained loans; it was a loan company only, and I think if my hon. friend will go back and trace the family Bible of the Motherwells he will find that there was no assistance of any other kind in eastern Ontario or in the county of Lanark.

Unless it was given to
soldiers, and that is another matter. There is just one other question on which I would-like to touch, and that is the argument that this measure has been endorsed twice by the House. The minister will remember that when the bill was before the House, so many suggestions were made going to the root of the matter which the minister promised to take into account, that we let the bill have first reading. maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
While not enthusiastic for
the bill I do think there is need for this class
Advances to Settlers

of legislation. Apparently it is opposed today by a number of hon. members because it is thought to be a measure for western Canada, and anything of that nature is opposed as a matter of course. It is taken that this measure is for western Canada entirely, and some hon. members have already expressed themselves as being tired of supporting the west by legislation of this kind. The people of the west have not particularly asked for it, but I do think that if a man wants to get on the land he should be assisted to do so. There are many such men to-day in the cities; they would be glad to go on a piece of land they could call their own if they could only be sure of having sufficient provisions until some improvements are made. That is a most worthy ambition, and I think it should be supported.
So far as I can see by the bill the loans will be given in instalments, as improvements are made. I really think this measure is needed; any scheme that will put the people back on the land should receive support. Why such a scheme is needed is, of course, another question. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) admits that if the industry paid its way there would be no need of such assistance. I only wish the right hon. gentleman would apply that principle to all industries in Canada. If an industry can pay its way. surely plenty of people will go in for that industry. The fact is that with the exception of agriculture all our industries have been built up by subventions, if my right hon. friend cares to use that word. I quite agree that you cannot 'build industries on subventions, as the right hon. gentleman has stated in this House many times during this session, and just now the industries so built are tumbling down on every side. This is a different scheme, simply a loan which is to be paid back within ten years, I think, of the time the settler makes entry.
I would like to answer an accusation which was made by the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan) when discussing this bill the other day. The hon. member seems to think that the more settlers there are in western Canada, the more the east will be called on to pay for the hauling of their wheat to the seaboard. He said that $6,000,000 was lost last year in that way-a statement made in utter ignorance of the facts. He also said that the east has borne the burdens of the west, long enough, but such is not the case. Anything that has ever been done in western Canada to further the settlement of great tracts of land has been to the benefit

of the east, and surely there can be no particular opposition to this bill, which -is so small in its scope. It will not be generally taken advantage of. In my estimation $1,000,000 would pay the first year's instalments, and I do not think more than that amount would be required in any single year. I do not think this country can do better than encourage our own people to go on the land and stay there. Other governments have been accused of being more willing to help foreigners than to help real Canadians, but here is a scheme which will put real Canadians on the land, and it certainly puzzles me to hear it opposed. I hope the minister will not see fit to withdraw the bill, and I trust that it will receive the support of the House.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I hope the minister will be good enough to withdraw this bill. Charming as is his personality, and able as he is to get legislation through this House, I can assure him that this is a measure which does not appeal to the House or the country. The great thing the people of this country are desiring to-day from the government is economy. People are burdened and sick of taxation; it bears down upon them, ruining industry and diminishing the employment of labour. Yet this government does not seem capable of realizing in the least the necessities of the hour.
Some hon. members have said they can sec no virtue at all in this bill. Looking at il from the standpoint of the Minister of the Interior and the political necessities of the hour, I can see considerable virtue in it. In the first place, the settler has to be approved by the minister or by his agent. Secondly, the improvements he makes on the land have also to be approved by the minister or by his agent. Thirdly, after he gets his loan sanctioned by the minister, the minister and his agents are going to step in and tell him how he is going to dispose of the money. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that no self-respecting man is going to bow the knee to any government or even accept a gift from them of one hundred or one hundred and sixty acres of land, with five hundred or one thousand dollars thrown in, and have himself tied up to the government in that manner that this bill would tie him up. It is an infringement on his liberties as a citizen of this country, and it is something the average man will not stand for.
This bill is lacking in two essentials to any successful settlement scheme. The first essential is to get the proper individual; that I think is the greatest asset in any undertaking.

Advances to Settlers
The minister says in effect: I am going out into the highways and byways to gather up men and put them on these lands. I am going to give them a hundred or an hundred and sixty acres of land and five hundred or one thousand dollars in money. Hon. gentlemen opposite are indeed living up to the name of their party and trying to prove themselves liberal. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this scheme was condemned as a failure when the minister informed us where he was going to get these settlers. Farming to-day, as everyone knows who has had anything to do with it-and I have spent some years on a farm myself-is not an occupation that anybody can make a success of, yet the minister says he is going to pick up, in the cities and towns and villages, people who have been failures, more or less, or they would not be leaving; transplant them on farms which he himself admits are second or third class farms and where the settler will have no earning power for the first three or four years. And he expects these people to make a success. The thing to my mind is utterly false in its conception, and in its operation will work to the detriment of this country. I am not a prophet, but if this scheme goes through I venture to say that it will have the soldier settlement scheme beaten by miles in the losses heaped upon this country, having regard to the capital invested. What has the settler to do? He goes out and locates a bit of land; he does a bit of work on it. The next thing he has to do is simply to get an inspector to pass on the land, and that is not very difficult. Then he gets his loan, and once he gets the money, what will he do? If he is sick of the farm, he will put the money in his pocket and walk off, and this government will be loaded with the loss.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the minister ought to withdraw his bill. There has been no demand for it from any of the provinces, unless probably the province from which the minister comes. It is unworkable. It is unfair relatively to the different provinces. I submit that it is also unfair to any man to put him on land where his earning capacity is going to be at a minimum for three or four years, load him with debt, and expect him to make good. I say here in the House of Commons, as I have said before, that the greatest curse that can be put on a young man is debt. I do not care whether he is in a profession, in business, or on the farm; the greater the debt you heap upon him, the greater injury you are doing him. Invariably you destroy his manhood, more or less, and destroy his power of developing, mentally at least. You are doing that man one of the greatest injuries
that you can possibly do to any man. I submit that in a country like this, with the millions and millions of acres of land that wre have, schemes of this kind are absolutely irrational and useless.
Mr. iLiETELLIER:	With your permission,
Mr. Chairman, I should like to inform the Minister of Immigration of the great advantage I derived in attending last fall a farmers' convention in the city of Montreal, under the auspices of the Catholic Agricultural Association of the province of Quebec. I am proud to say that this question was brought up at the convention by some of the real farmers of the province of Quebec. Fathers of large families had been asking whether it would not be possible for the association to pass a resolution urging the government to pass legislation with a view to helping those farmers who were anxious to establish their sons on farms in areas where the timber had been cut by the industrial companies and where the land was really first-class for farming. Many of them claimed that if they could obtain the least help from the government they could keep their sons at home, and I know of many families in that situation, Mr. Chairman, in my constituency, especially in Martinville, Compton, and Marsboro. I really believe that if this legislation is passed and well administered, if the settlers are chosen in good faith, if farmers or the sons of farmers who have been brought up on the farm and have learned the most practical way of farming are put on these lands, the government will obtain the very best results.
Some hon. gentlemen have referred to mistakes that have been made in the past in connection with legislation similar to this. As an illustration I would mention the case of a number of returned soldiers who were established on farms. Many of them were without any real qualifications for farming and were lacking entirely in experience. A number of cases, illustrating their utter lack of experience, came to my own notice where the soldier settler paid as much as $125 or $150 for cattle that were not worth $60. In the case of the present legislation it would seem that the mistakes of the past have been guarded against. I would ask the minister, therefore, to insist upon the bill going through, and would urge hon. members to support the measure. I am sure that if the settlers chosen are men of experience in farming and the legislation bill is well administered, it will be productive of the happiest results.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
There has been a good deal of discussion of this proposition both in the resolution stage and on the bill as it is now before the committee. It is unfortunate, perhaps, that our discussion in the resolution stage was not more full and complete than it was. I propose to discuss in a general way the object which this bill has in view. It appears to me to be one of those schemes that look very well on paper, but when we come to apply it to actual conditions and to see just how it will work out, we find many defects and weaknesses in it. The minister has given the House and the committee a great deal of information, but I do not recall that he cited any schemes like this that had ever been tried out and had proven to be successful. We would be more ready to receive the proposal favourably if we had not recently been called upon to consider the revaluation of soldier settlers' land, in connection with a scheme which was originally well conceived, which was surrounded with all the precautions that could possibly be taken and which had the very worthy and desirable object of settling our returned soldiers on the land. We are now called upon to make a revaluation of those lands, and there is no doubt whatever that we are facing a very large reduction in the indebtedness due to the Dominion in that connection.
What is the scheme that is now before us? It is a plan to settle people upon lands that have been found undesirable, lands that have been passed over, lands that are inferior to other lands in the same locality. I cannot think of any greater handicap that could be placed upon a settler than to induce him to go upon land that is not likely in the near future to yield him a reasonable return, land that will be difficult to develop, difficult to cultivate and difficult to make productive. A second handicap is placed upon him by setting an indebtedness against that land. If a farmer is to succeed, the first essential is that he be placed upon land that is good in quality, that is easily developed and that will speedily bring him a return.
There does not appear to be any real general demand for this legislation. So far as I have been able to ascertain, no province has made any special request for it, and there have been no petitions or anything in the nature of a volume of public opinion asserting itself in favour of it. The further we go the more lukewarm we become in our attitude

toward this proposition. There is another objection which I think is pretty generally admitted by all parties in this House, namely, that several of the provinces will derive no benefit at all from the proposal because of the conditions prevailing in those provinces. I think that if any money is appropriated for the purposes set forth in this bill it should be divided among the provinces on the basis of population, and there should not be available for anjr one province any more than its fair share on that basis. The amount first suggested, $5,000,000, has been reduced to $1,000,000. That sum, if apportioned in this way, is so small as to produce practically no desirable results.
The scheme is full of complications and of difficulties, and in a way is in conflict with provincial jurisdiction. Priorities of claims and all sorts of liens for taxes and other equities and rights arise, all of which will be difficult of settlement. It does appear to me however, that the greatest, the most serious objection of all is that we are undertaking to place settlers on undesirable lands, thus handicapping them: we are inducing them to undertake a venture in which they are not likely to succeed. And more than that, we are placing them under an obligation from which it will be difficult for them to free themselves. For that reason I do not feel inclined to support the scheme just now.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I do not
intend to speak at any great length in opposition to the measure, but I do feel that it is not one that will serve the purpose of securing settlers to take up land. I do not think that $1,000 in the way of loan to the average Canadian citizen is going to assist in getting the right sort of man to go on the land. I do not know anything about the nature of the soil in western Canada, -where this scheme proposes to place settlers, but I do know that the average man who wants to go on a farm and cultivate it will not be induced to do so by the prospect of getting a loan of $1,000 from the Dominion government, even at the low rate of interest of five per cent. And so far as getting immigrants from outside is concerned, immigrants from the continent of Europe, I hardly think that a loan of $500 will be the means of bringing into this country the kind of agriculturists we desire. I believe, of course, that we should make every effort to secure more immigrants, for undoubtedly we need an increased population. At the same time, we want the right kind of people to come in and not merely those who are to be assisted in

Advances to Settlers
this particular way. Any man coming from the Old Land who has not sufficient money to start farming on his own account will certainly not be assisted by a loan of $500. Such an advance will not place him in a position to cultivate land in the Canadian west, or, for that matter, in any other province of Canada. It seems to me therefore that, as a means of colonizing the country, this measure will prove utterly futile.
I would stress another point which I have mentioned before. It is this: The farming community is about the only section of our population that desires competition and more competition in its particular business. That is something that is being discussed in this House. Members of the Progressive group, when they first came into this House in 1921, frequently referred to the necessity of getting more people to take up land in Canada, but I am interested to observe of late that there is a tendency on the part of these hon. gentlemen to ignore that aspect of the question. They are not talking the same way now. I suspect that they are coming to the conclusion that there are other spheres of activity in Canada in which immigrants would be of more use to the country, especially when we are producing from the land more than the people can consume.
In my opinion the government will only be adding to the debt of the country by putting this measure into force. It will be absolutely of no avail in building up a sound yeomanry that could be of value to the rest of Canada.
I am therefore disposed to vote against the bill. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) seems to be satisfied that this legislation will advance the interests of the west. He probably knows more about that than I do and I should take his word, to some extent at all events. I think, however, that it is possible for even a minister of the crown to be mistaken.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
The object of this bill is to
secure settlers for just two or three of the provinces, for I cannot see how it will get settlers to go on the land in other parts of the Dominion. In the older provinces the conditions are to-day, as they have always been, such as would readily lend themselves to legislation of this kind to encourage immigration. I can speak, of course, only for the province from which I come. In that province the settler can obtain land merely by applying for it, and the conditions under which he gets his title are very simple. Practically all he has to do is to make a home for himself : he builds a house on the land, clears a few acres, and that gives him his title.
I do not see how that province can be assisted by means of this bill in the matter of securing immigrants.
We had in our province some years ago an act which I presume is still on the statute books, but which has fallen into disrepute. At any rate it is no longer invoked. That act provides that the government shall advance money to settlers to enable them to clear their land for cultivation. Let me show how it has worked out-and my opinion is that the legislation now before us will have the same effect. In passing, I may observe that I have not yet acquired that confidence in my fellowmen which, judging from the debate that has taken place in this House this afternoon, seems to prevail among certain members of parliament. The individual is apt to be unreliable when it comes to collateral security, and in addition to that he is well endowed with ingenuity. Now, if under this bill money is advanced on the basis of weak collateral, what will happen? The government will be saddled with lands that are of no use. We already have an illustration of that, in the case of the rural credits system. Why is it that so much of the money lent out under that system has not come back to the provinces? Simply because the collateral is weak, and you cannot force payment. That is just what is going to happen here if I can read the bill aright. We are to advance money on land to a farmer or a person of any other occupation, and he will use that money just as he likes. The government probably will not have any control over the money, but he will. Whether he ever returns it or not will depend a good deal on how matters go with him; if easy, he will return the money, otherwise he is not likely to do so. In the case of our provincial government, as I mentioned a few moments ago, this happened- and it will happen in this case I guess-numbers of settlers had been on the land for several years and had cleared up five acres or more, but they had never done enough work to get their deeds. When the rural credits scheme came into force some ingenious men saw' a chance to make money, and they gave those settlers a hundred dollars or less, and they soon got title to their lands. Then what happened? Why, it was no trouble to go to , the board and get anywhere from $500 up to $3,000 and more, with the result that to-day the province has got those farms. There is another phase which I may bring to the attention of the committee. The province was granting land to practically any man that would ask for it provided he complied with the requirements, the most important of which were that he must be a. resident of the prov-
Advances to Settlers

ince and be twenty-one years of age. Such a man could get land virtually for nothing. Subsequently he got his title to the land and borrowed money on his holding. The government soon found they had better get out of the business; they did so, but not without a good deal of scandal. To-day the province is out of pocket and somebody else has got the money. That to my mind is just what is going to happen under this bill.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Will my hon. friend tell me what province he refers to-New Brunswick?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
You did not know I came from there! I would not say anything about the prairie provinces or the Maritime provinces generally, or for that matter the older provinces, Quebec and Ontario, that I aru saying about my own province. I do not think Quebec will benefit very much by this measure, for it has already a splendid act of its own. In New Brunswick we hope to get similar legislation at this session of the legislature. The gist of the Quebec act is that when you accept a man's application for a homestead you allow him ten dollars an acre to clear it, and I am sure that is better encouragement than lending him money. If he works and clears his land he gets ten dollars an acre, which helps him to live while he is preparing his farm for cultivation; afterwards he can provide for himself.
Now, with regard to the fifteen mile limit, it would not be of any use in my province, nor for that matter in any of the older provinces, because there is no good land anywhere near the railways but what is owned now. When you talk of having miles to travel in the prairies, I do not think you really know anything about distance. Many of our farmers are fifty miles away from a railway, but they rarely buy automobiles to get backwards and forwards.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: How do they bring their wheat to market?

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
They bring their produce to
market by water. So I think that so far as my province is concerned this bill will be practically of no use whatever. After all, what is it going to amount to? At one time the amount to be advanced was placed at 85,000,000. Well, if I can judge aright, I do not think that would be too big a sum, for everybody will go after easy money. We will all take a hand in it, we will be there at the beginning while the money is available, not at the end when it is about exhausted. But what then, who is going to take the burden of debt that will be left on our 
shoulders? I think it would be well to confine the operation of this measure to the two or three provinces that are going to specially benefit by it.

speechtext:

If a man goes on the land, spends his own time and money making certain improvements, and increases the value of the crown domain to a point that justifies t'he minister in advancing a loan to him, is the minister going to send somebody to say to that man: You can do just this and that with the money we are giving you now for the work you have already performed? The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario raised the question and it bears out what was said by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) this afternoon, namely, that you could not get men to go on some of those lands unless you gave them some inducement. If the prospect of this loan is an inducement, the probabilities are that the man who goes on the land will incur liabilities to

someone else. He will effect loans; he will secure supplies from merchants to enable him to carry on until he makes those improvements. After the improvements are made the minister comes along under another provision in the bill and says to the man: We are going to direct you as to just how you are to spend the money; you may pay this indebtedness and leave the other one unpaid, and so on; or you may not pay any of them but you piust go on anid make some more improvements. There is the confusion in connection with this matter. The difference between this legislation and the plan under which the soldier land settlement was carried out is that under the latter the money was advanced for the purpose of making improvements, to buy stock and so on. In this case the man goes on the land the crown assigns to him, spends his time and money and improves it up to a certain point that causes the board or the minister to feel safe in making him a loan on the strength of the improvements already made. Surely if he was capable in the first instance of directing his own affairs and making improvements to the point where he could secure a loan, he should be given a free hand to go ahead and spend the money advanced. If he runs away with the money, the government 'have already the improvements on the land. I can readily understand the minister does not expect anything of that sort; nevertheless he is imposing that unfair hardship on a free man, and so long as you undertake to keep these men in a state of vassalage

that is exactly what their position will be-they are not going to be free men. If you find the man who is a sufficiently good moral risk to justify a loan, surely you have the Canadian citizen whom you can trust to spend the money you lend to him in the same way that he has spent his own money in making such improvements as justified the making of the loan in the first instance.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the difficulties of the Minister in tiying to satisfy the committee in framing this bill. On the one hand fear is expressed that the security will not be sufficient and that the government will lose a lot of money; on the other hand, the minister is exhorted to use all means to enable settlers to secure money with the greatest facility. If the minister tries to harmonize these two views I do not know where he is going to end. I am in favour of the principle of this bill, but I am distinctly opposed to the policy of its application. I expressed that view on a previous occasion, and the minister will pardon me if I express it again. At the outset, however, I may congratulate the minister on the fact that this is the first attempt ever ' made in this House, it appears to me, to bring forward any policy to assist settlers in getting on the land. I can at least congratulate the minister on that, and for the very reason that I sympathize with the proposal, I am most anxious to see it on a sounder basis than it is at present.
I agree with a good many of the criticisms that land which is not suitable for cultivation, land not suitable to be taken up at all. is the kind of land that will be homesteaded under this scheme. A settler who will not take up homestead land at present, looking od this
Advances to Settlers

loan as a bonus, will take up some of this land and endeavour to make some improvements on it, and it appears to me that the homestead land available for settlement in western Canada to-day is not of a very good quality. There is very little of it except in some districts that have recently been opened up by branch 'lines, in which cases I 'believe there is some good land. I believe I can speak with some authority on this question, because a large .part of my constituency borders on the bush land, and I know something about the settlement in those districts. There is no doubt that a great many men under the stimulus of these loans will take up some of this homestead land but I venture to predict now that within five years at least 50 per cent of those men will have abandoned the land. I think there is no question about that. If the minister occupies his present position five years from now, I feel perfectly safe in predicting that he will come back to this House and admit that this scheme is a failure, from two standpoints. It will be a failure from the standpoint of assisting settlers, and from the financial point of view as well. But because I am anxious to see something done to assist settlers I would plead with the minister as I pleaded with him on a previous occasion, to make this act apply to purchased land, where facilities are already provided; land close to the railways, where we have schools, roads, elevators, stores and everything already there. We have millions of acres of that kind of land in western 'Canada, where everything is already provided.
The minister stated in 'introducing this resolution that the main object was to thicken up the settlements. That is the very thing this bill is not going to do; it will spread the settlements out into the hinteriand a little further than they are to-day. I believe if this were made to apply to purchased land, and if assistance were given settlers in buying land, not only would ample security be provided, but something would be done in a substantial way to assist settlement.
I know the question will 'be asked' as to how we can make a loan on land purchased with very little, and in some cases perhaps nothing, paid on it. Land can be secured in western Canada to-day 'by very small cash payments, and if those selling the land are prepared to assist in the operation of this plan, they will be prepared to permit the government to take a first mortgage on the land for $1,000 or whatever amount is advanced. and take security themselves by a

second' mortgage. In every case of that.kind the land will be worth a great deal more than the money advanced 'by the government, and the security will be better than the security at present held by most of the loan companies.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: The land in my constituency to which I referred is as good a class of homestead land as is available in any part of Canada. Why? Because they had incurred liabilities during the three year period when they were earning their patents, and it was to pay off the liabilities incurred by the purchase of the odd cow, the horses and the machinery that they had accumulated in that time that they required the loan. All I have in mind here is to avoid the necessity of doing that. The man will be starting on land where he does not require a large number of horses or a large outfit of machinery, but can start in a very moderate way. That is all I had in mind, but please remember that it is not contemplated to lend money on poor land.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Why should the government lend $1,000 to a Canadian citizen and only $500 to a man who is not a Canadian citizen? How does the difference affect the security?

speechtext:
What the minister says
is perfectly correct, that the bulk of the homestead land in western Canada was taken up by people who had very little money. But I want to point out this, that this homesteading was done at a period when we were building thousands of miles of railway in western Canada, and a great majority of these homesteaders simply filed on their land and then went out and worked on the railway or with a building gang, building elevators or stores in the little towns that were growing up all over the prairie. In that way they were able to earn enough money to give them a start on their homestead. There are very few men who have made a success in western Canada who ever went on their homestead without any money to start with, unless they were able to stay with it by going out in the summer time and working elsewhere. I have been twenty years in western Canada, and I have pioneered in many new districts, and I know very few men to-day who when they first came in and homesteaded were able to establish themselves on the land without going out and earning money in the summer time. But those conditions do not obtain in western Canada to-day. We are not building any more railways now, and instead of there being a shortage of labour, there is a surplus. Very

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Before the minister redrafts the clause, may I ask him with regard to provincial crown lands for which temporary titles are given by the government which do not carry the full ownership which letters patent do. Then if the settler does not comply with the requirements of the depart-mennt, his title is forfeited. He may have made some improvements on the land, but all that is lost to him. Now suppose a new settler comes in and is prepared to take up that land; would he be entitled under this' law to a loan on the improvements made by his predecessor which have advanced the value of the property, but which of course were not made by the present settler on the land when occupied by him? I think the present wording of the clause would prevent the loaning of money to any new settler who would take over a partly improved crown land farm that had been abandoned, because the improvements would not have been made by him when occupying the land. If he received the encouragement of a loan he might go on with the improvements and finally make of this land a real homestead; in fact, we have many homesteads in the province of Quebec of that nature. It is said, in fact, in many regions that the first settler is never the permanent occupant of the land. Very often the letters patent are taken out by the new settler who comes in and inherits the improvements made by his predecessor, but, after all, he continues to improve the land, and implants there a family, and finally the Whole community benefits by it. I know of many lands in my own constituency, as well as in other parts, that are presently crown lands because the letters patent have never been issued; the lands were taken up by settlers some years ago, and abandoned. speechtext: How is the immigrant to get $500? Because he must make the improvements himself, and the loan can be made only on such improvements. The immigrant is in England and can by no possibility have made any improvements.

speechtext:
My hon.
friend knows a good deal of recruiting is done in the Old Country for placing people upon the land. I speak particularly of soldier settlers. The initial stages are all taken in the Old Country. The same thing would apply in this case. If the settler comes here entirely unhampered, as a matter of course he becomes a Canadian citizen in five years.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: An immigrant cannot get a loan under this bill, and no immigrant is going to come here and borrow $500 within a year if he can stay one week over the year and get $1,000.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
The minister, in answer to the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) who, I am sorry, has gone out for the moment, has taken a position that, as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) says, throws the door open very much wider than I think he contemplates. What the hon. member for Labelle said is, I think very largely true, namely, that the original entrant or settler on crown lands in a large part of northern Ontario and northern Quebec is not the final settler and the man
who gets the patent for the land. There is a very definite reason for that. I will speak more particularly of northern Ontario, because I have lived there for almost forty-five years. Men go on the land there not for the purpose of settling on it at all, but in order to take off during this period the most valuable crop that the land will ever have on it, and that is the timber. A settler on crown lands in Ontario and Quebec is entitled to all the timber on the land, spruce, maple and so on, excepting white and red pine. These men go on the land; they 'make a certain amount of improvements; they build a house or put up a camp to live in while they are there, and they cultivate a certain quantity of the land; but instead of their work constituting an improvement they have very much depreciated the original value of the land by removing the timber. If the minister is going to lend money to the second entrant in a case of that kind, he is not lending money because the value of the land has been improved. The land is not as valuable as it was before. As I said a moment ago, the most valuable crop the land can have on it in any one period of time is the original crop of timber. There are thousands of such cases where the timber has been removed according to an enumeration which was taken across all northern Ontario; and my information is that the same condition prevails very largely in northern Quebec as to the timber on the land and as to the type of settler who goes in there. The timber exploiter in many cases takes off the timber, and instead of the crown having an added security, it will never again get on that land anything as valuable as what the man has taken off. If the minister is going to give somebody else a loan on the strength of that, he is not getting any security at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I think a
very much wider construction than is intended is being put upon the bill, judging from the questions that have been asked with respect to the second entrant upon crown land. What I had in mind was simply a case where a homesteader, as we call him in the west, goes upon land and abandons it. That happens in a considerable number of cases. If there are upon the land improvements which are always of a meagre character, we charge the second entrant with those improvements. I can conceive of a situation all through the older provinces where, just as my hon. friend has said, the most valuable crop the land will ever produce has gone and the lands are abandoned. I can say at once that no loan of any character would be made upon land of that description. The land itself must be good land.
Advances to Settlers

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
This is the best of
land.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I do not
know the circumstances, but if they are the best of lands it is a strange thing that they should be lying idle with no one in possession of them. The lands must be good lands before they come under the provisions of this legislation. It is likely that there will not be many cases in which consideration will be given for a loan to a second entrant, because as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has pointed out, the intention of this measure is to get new settlers on new lands. I can conceive of cases where 160 or ICO acres of land have been taken up and abandoned, and if it is good land someone else #will immediately apply. Improvements of some value may have been effected that the present applicant will have to improve further before he will be given consideration for a loan. As regards widespread applications, hon. members will please forget that, because that is not the intention of the government under this legislation.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
The minister himself seems to
be in some doubt as to the construction to place upon the matter we are now dealing with, namely, the words "on the security of improvements made by such settler." One would think, from a reading of the section that the intention was that nobody could make application other than the settler Who himself, or by his agents at all events, had made the improvements. I am aware that if this legislation has to be construed in the future any declarations or statements that we make in this House will make no difference. But if there is any doubt about the matter- and from what the minister says there seems to be some doubt about it-it should be placed beyond peradventure.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Since this
discussion has arisen-and I see the possibility of its spreading out into wide dimensions-as that is not the purpose at all I may have to come back to the House and confine the provisions of the bill strictly to first settlers and crown lands.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
I would not say that it
should be made applicable to first settlers only.	It seems to me that the only
person entitled to a loan is the settler who makes the improvements, whether he be the first or the second entrant. But I would certainly be opposed to the legislation if it was to entitle the second entrant, who has done nothing whatever upon the land but who gets possession because of an abandonment,

to get a loan of $500 or $1,000 on the strength of what somebody else has done. That would be absurd. As I read the bill it does not mean that, but I am making this criticism because of the more or less indefinite attitude the minister has taken upon it. He seemed to think that the door was open to that construction. I certainly do not think it is, but if there is any doubt about the matter and if the clause is to be redrafted, as I understand it is, it ought, I think, to be made perfectly clear that it is to relate to the improvements made by the applicant and by nobody else.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
The act
clearly was to apply to the first entrant upon a given piece of crown land. I can see where we might make it apply to the second-
* Mr. BOYS: Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: The intention was of course to settle unoccupied crown lands.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Very well; and if the land is abandoned it is unoccupied.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: That is true. The difficulty is that in giving way in one particular, pressure is brought to bear upon you to give waj' further. I am thoroughly in accord with the suggestion that the idea was to. confine it absolutely to the original applicant, and to unoccupied crown lands.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: It does not necessarily follow that it should be confined to the original occupant, so long as it is confined to the improvements that have been made by the present applicant whether he be the first, second, third or fourth person to occupy the land.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
My hon.
friend knows of course that Wherever a homesteader has settled on land he has made some improvements.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: There might be misrepresentation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: Not always. The applicant, generally speaking, makes improvements for which usually he gets no credit.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
The minister misunderstands
me. There might be some misrepresentation by the second or the third entrant in regard to improvements he alleges to have been made by himself. He might suggest that he had made some improvements wrhile in reality he had made none. '

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: When you confine it definitely to the improvements effected by the applicant himself and by no one else, you are apt to have trouble. Clearly, as I see it, the intention of the bill as drafted is that the provision shall apply to unimproved crown lands, and to the first applicant.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Subsection
(b) of section 3 provides for a loan:
To a settler, other than, a Canadian citizen, an amount not exceeding five hundred dollars.
Is it the intention to make a loan to a foreigner coming here to settle on land before he has taken out his papers and become a naturalized British subject?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:

answer that question rather carefully. I think I am correct in saying yes, but I may add that the settler cannot obtain his patent until he is a British subject. That safeguard is provided. .

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: The minister, I think, said that before, and I understand that part of it. My objection would be to making the loan to such an applicant at all. I do not think that any man coming to Canada should come within the provisions of this bill until he has become a naturalized British subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext: I shall look into that point carefully. Before making application. however, the settler is required to declare his intention of becoming a British subject.

maintopic: ADVANCES TO SETTLERS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
How would this provision
affect orientals and Doukhobors? Usually the Poukhobor is interested mainly in getting the timber off the land, which he then abandons.

The oriental does not come under the bill.

man at Halifax supervises the work at Yarmouth and North Sydney as well. Probably that is the reason why he has been classified as a supervising examiner, but of course this title has been given him by the Civil Service Commission.

speechtext:
The minister stated that
there has been no examiner at Yarmouth for a whole year. Could not that $1,400 be very well dispensed with? That is a small item, perhaps, but if these other men could do the work that amount would be saved.
