speechtext:
In answer to my hon.
friend I am informed that the examiner at Halifax has been requested several times to go to Yarmouth. I would hesitate to close this office, because I am informed that the people in that vicinity are anxious to keep the office, and it has been profitable and advantageous to those interested in such matters. At all events, I am ready to take into consideration the very friendly representations made by my hon. friends opposite.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
What does the minister
think about the position at Nelson?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: That position is vacant at the present time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Has it been vacant during the whole year?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Then the same thing which applies to Yarmouth would apply also to Nelson.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: If the $1,400 was not paid at Yarmouth this year, how comes it there is no difference between the $20,000 of the previous year and the $20,000 of last year?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: We are asking for the same amount as last year, but this does not represent the expenditure.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: What amount was expended last year?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
We spent $15,952, up to
February 28th last.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
How many vacant positions
were there?
Mr. CARDIN':	Three, one at Yarmouth,
one at Selkirk, Manitoba, and one at Nelson, British Columbia. The salary at Nelson and Selkirk is small, only $600. At Yarmouth it is $1,440.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
What does the examiner at
Yarmouth do to earn $1,400? The place has been closed a year. How many examinations did he have to make?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
I have not the number of
examinations which he made last year.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
I
observe from the Auditor General's report that the amount spent last year was $19,994.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: That is for 1924-25.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Would the minister state what the duties of the supervising examiner are? I understand that candidates for the positions of mate and captain come before examiners, and are examined by them. What is the work of the supervising examiner, who does not see the candidates at all?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
The supervising examiner
checks the papers of the examiners at the other places. The examination papers at Yarmouth, for example, are forwarded to the supervising examiner at Halifax, who checks them up. He supervises the work of the officers in the smaller ports, like Yarmouth and North Sydney.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Are the certificates that are granted issued by the supervising examiner?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: :	The examiner at Yarmouth, for example, sends in his report to the supervising examiner at Halifax, who checks the papers and forwards them to Ottawa, and the certificate is issued at the department here after all the documents have been passed on and approved by the supervising examiner at Halifax.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Could there not be some competent officer in the department here to do the supervising, instead of the supervising officer who does not see the candidates at all?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: We have officers in the department checking even the reports of the supervising examiner.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
If
the supervising examiner does not see the candidates at all, it would seem to me that some of this work must be superfluous, because the report he makes to the minister has to be examined by officials in the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
If the work of the
supervising examiner at Halifax, for instance, is that of checking the reports of the men who actually examine the candidates, then forwarding them to Ottawa for rechecking, surely instead of having one supervising examiner at Halifax with an office and an office staff and another at Toronto with an office and an office staff-not actually examining candidates but simply scrutinizing fifty or sixty examination papers annually, sent in to him by the
men who actually make the examination-the minister could save a little money by having only one supervising examiner stationed at Ottawa, to whom all these reports could be sent in the first place. Why send the papers from Yarmouth to Halifax, and from Port Arthur or Collingwood to Toronto, to be checked, and then send them to Ottawa to be rechecked? Set the examinations, if you will, and then at Toronto, Collingwood, Owen Sound, and other places where you have scores of captains doing nothing when their ships are laid up, and who would be glad to act as examiners, have these local men do the work and send in their reports to one supervising examiner at Ottawa for the whole country. The minister could save a little money here, at least, and the virtue of saving is a very good virtue to begin to practise at some point.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
Even if we could find
somebody in Toronto and elsewhere to take charge of the examinations, they would not work for nothing; we should have to pay them. I might point out that these supervising officers not only supervise the reports of other officers, but they also act as examiners themselves; in fact their most important work is taking charge of the examinations in the more important ports. They supervise, in addition, the work done in the less important places, but their main duty is to carry on a very much greater number of examinations themselves.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
Is there a greater
number of applicants for certificates as masters and mates in Toronto than in Port Arthur, Fort William, Sault Ste. Marie, Collingwood, or any of these ports out of which boats on the Great Lakes run? Why should it be necessary to have a supervising examiner conduct the examinations at one port, and an ordinary captain-for that is what they are, practical men who know their business-make the examinations at some other port? The class of work done in both cases is just the same, so why should one man get $2,500 a year and be given a stenographer and an office, and another man somewhere else be paid only half that amount-because the minister has stated that the salary ranges from $600 to $1,450 and so on? Why make this variation? If you want a supervising examiner, why not have one at Ottawa for the whole country?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
The supervising examiners
have much more work to do. The supervising examiner at Toronto, for instance, has recommended the issuing of certificates for 43 masters, although he has examined a greater number than that, and 25 mates. In Kingston, for example, eleven masters and fourteen mates passed their examination compared with forty-

Supply-Marine and Fisheries
three masters and twenty-five mates, at Toronto. At Port Arthur only two masters passed the examination and only one mate. So the wo.rk the examiners have to do at these smaller places is not so heavy as the work which has to be performed in a large city like Toronto.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
I should like to ask the
minister for the third time if it is not possible to cut out some of these places? There is an examination held in Kingston, one in Toronto, one in Collingwood, one at the Soo, and one at Port Arthur.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
The supervising examiner
for the Great Lakes division not only conducts the examination at Toronto but also visits other places in the province. At Collingwood we have Captain Coles, but he receives a salary of only 8600. Outside of conducting examinations he gives lectures on navigation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Surely the minister does not seriously contend that all these officers are kept busy examining students during the twelve months when there are only forty candidates at one place, twenty at another and thirty at another. Why, there is not enough work combined to keep one man busy two months. I should like the minister to take this matter a little more seriously. It is a small matter, it is true, but there is a duplication of offices and salaries in .Ontario at least that is absolutely unwarranted. The minister simply receives the suggestion with a shake of his head, as though it were of no importance whatever. If he has an examiner in Toronto who goes to Collingwood, a distance of only three hours by train, why is it necessary to have another examiner in the latter port? What is the sense of this duplication at every little port around the lakes? After all it only represents about one man's job for a year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
I am afraid I could not
venture to close the office at Toronto without incurring very serious criticism from the navigation companies. They are desirous of maintaining the office so that they may obtain properly qualified masters and mates. The Toronto office is really doing a very important work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: I am not asking you to close the office at Toronto, I am asking what is the sense of maintaining seven or eight of these offices in the province of Ontario.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
There is really only one office having jurisdiction over the Great Lakes, and that is the Toronto office. But

the supervising examiner holds examinations at smaller places.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Did you not tell us that you had an official at Collingwood?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: There is one there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: And at the Soo and at Port Arthur?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: There is only one at Collingwood. That official receives a small salary and, as I have just stated, delivers lectures on navigation outside his other duties.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that the minister has not increased his staff since 1924-5? You still have a man with a stenographer in Toronto, and you have a man in Collingwood?
. Mr. CARDIN: Absolutely.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: And the chief examiner conducts examinations at other points in the province?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: The examiner at Toronto does.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: The provision made does not seem excessive.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
If there are only two
men, why the need of estimates to the amount of $20,000?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: That $20,000 is for the whole country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Yes, $20,000 for the whole work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: You have been telling us that two men only are doing the work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: No, that was the work of the Great Lakes division of Toronto.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: We have to defend the interests of Ontario against my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: What is the cost of the Port Arthur office?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: What class of stenographer have you in Toronto? The salary you pay is $600. That does not seem enough for a stenographer in that city.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: The salary is $780, the salary of a regular stenographer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: That is not as much as other stenographers get in government departments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
This amount has been fixed by the Civil Service Commission for the work performed there.

Supply-Marine and Fisheries

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Is the stenographer employed all the time, or just temporarily?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: All the time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: It is a very low salary.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: I rather sympathize with the minister in his efforts to enlighten my agricultural friends behind me.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: There would be no objection in the Maritime provinces if the minister closed up all these offices on the lakes. They are only fresh-water sailors up there, and perhaps seldom out of sight of land. For the enlightenment of my hon. friends behind me, and of others, I may say that the offices in the Maritime provinces are necessary. Let me illustrate why. A young man goes to sea. After he has been at sea for a year or two years he goes up for examination as second mate. He takes a month, two months, or three months as the case may be to attend a navigation school, and then he goes up for his second mate's ticket. If he passes the examination he gets his ticket. He goes to sea again and after having served a certain length of time and obtained a certificate that he has served for that period as second mate, he again goes to the navigation school for whatever time may be necessary. Then he goes up for examination for his first mate's certificate. Having succeeded "in obtaining his certificate he goes again to sea and passes a certain specified time as first mate. He comes back with the required certificate and attends the navigation school for a further period. Then he presents himself for examination and in the event of his being successful is given his ticket as a master. These offices in the Maritime provinces are absolutely necessary. A man may have been at sea on a foreign voyage for six or nine months and then his ship goes into Sydney or into some other port in the Cape Breton district. It is not reasonable that he should be required to go to Halifax to undergo examination. It is for that reason that examining offices have been established at the outports of Sydney and Yarmouth. The only objection I have in the matter is this: If the office of examiner at Yarmouth was vacant during the whole of last year it is something which should not have happened -it is a positive hardship. I object to any reduction in the vote for the Maritime provinces, but I am not concerned to any extent whatever as to the fate of the Ontario examining offices.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: I asked the minister previously what the cost of the Port Arthur office was.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: There is no office at Port Arthur. The supervising examiner goes there and conducts the examination himself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
The minister
sends a man there to examine two or three people, I understand, two masters and one mate?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Who is the supervising examiner at Vancouver?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Captain L. H. Lindsay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
How long has he held the
office?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Two years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Who was the former officer?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Captain Eddie.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: What is the salary paid?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
Does he hold any other position under the government?
M'r. CARDIN: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Does he give his whole time to the work?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext:
He is not allowed to do
any other work?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES

Item agreed to.
Investigation into wrecks, $6,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: Will the minister explain this item? The reason I want to know is because I have been trying to have a little wreck removed at the mouth of the Nottawasaga river, and I want to make sure that has been provided for this year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: I am informed it has been removed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MARINE AND FISHERIES
speechtext: I am glad to be able to congratulate the government on accomplishing one thing at all events.

Item agreed to.
